headline: Our test harnesses have been quietly burning display numbers for five days, and the guard we added last week is what made it certain.
matters: 1,500 stale directories and 100 dead lock files had built up since the 25th, and every leaked lock permanently burns an X display number so every later test run scans longer before it can start. It is now cleaned up automatically as each run ends. The residue already on the machine is still there and still growing — from other projects' test runs, not this one.
detail: O20+O23, merge 055bff40 pushed. Cause: /usr/bin/xvfb-run has no trap, so its whole cleanup sits after the command line and is skipped whenever the wrapper is signalled — which is what killTree does on every teardown, so O16's orphan fix guaranteed this leak. Two leak rates, the uncounted one 17x the counted: tempdirs leak on every teardown, locks/sockets only on abrupt ones. Both rows were wrong: no .sh starts an X server (the four unguarded launchers are .mjs), and two .sh DO launch by proxy. reapDisplays() is scoped to artifacts named by processes inside a tree the harness launched. THE PARCEL'S REAL LESSON: boundSocketPaths() failed OPEN against its own docstring — an empty Set meant both 'I could not look' and 'nothing is bound', so gate 3 would invert from a refusal into a permission and leave the never-reap list as the only thing protecting the owner's desktop socket; latent, not live. Found by an overseer poison that came back GREEN because gate 3 was covering for gate 1. Now a null sentinel read as gate 0, refuse everything loudly. Two further poisons re-planted independently by the overseer post-fix, each firing in exactly one row. A third silently no-op'd against a changed declaration and returned a clean 20/20 — proof-the-edit-landed is now the rule before any plant is believed. Merged tree: xvfb-reap 20/20, guard checker 166 classified / 0 failures / 0 unmeasurable, node 5817/0/7, tsc clean.

headline: Correction to tonight's leak note: the leftover files are our own, not another project's, and I said otherwise.
matters: I told you the leak was still growing from someone else's test runs. It was growing from mine — I had deliberately broken the cleanup three times to prove the fix works, and the files that appeared were the proof. The cleanup itself is real and still landed. I also called the leftover files a speed hazard; measured, the cost is under a millisecond per run, so that was overstated.
detail: Corrects the 02:51Z entry and re-scopes queue row O34; nothing in merge 055bff40 changes. Seraph challenged the suite-wide claim and was right to; its own relayed figure (locks zero) was wrong — locks are 108, sockets 91, tempdirs 1522, 0 live Xvfb, re-measured with find. THE ERROR WAS INSTRUMENTAL: I reasoned from a DELTA (+17 in every class across two rounds) where an ABSOLUTE with timestamps was available the whole time, and a delta cannot see its own author. The fingerprint settles it — every lock today falls in a burst of exactly 17 at 9-10s intervals with a ~25s tail, six identical bursts, one inside my own session window. One producer, aurora's own harness. Two traps banked: find -printf %TY is LOCAL time so the '08-29' bucket is today (02:54 UTC = 22:54 EDT); and my launch-count grep counted string mentions, so the CHECKER — which greps for those strings — topped it at exactly 17 and matched the burst size by coincidence. Still open: the sweep (foreground, held while peers are live) and 6 unguarded-untracked launchers in the owner's tree that the landed fix does not reach.

headline: Four things in the editor claimed something was alive when they could not know it — including a test that rejected every correct emulator.
matters: A test guarding your playtest runs had been aborting on any up-to-date emulator and passing only on a stale one. The editor also could not tell you which emulator answered it, so a session against the wrong one failed later and further away, looking like features that stopped working. And a tool reported success for a background assignment that never reaches the game.
detail: O26+O28+O32+O33, merge 6da97049 pushed. One class: an artifact asserting a liveness it cannot know. O26 pinned the served method COUNT at 35 and threw otherwise; the real count moved 35->52->53->55 in a day, twice while the agent worked, so the check was inverted against its purpose — now derived from the methods actually called. O28 the discovery file outlived every process it named (verified live at dispatch: a dead pid on disk); writer cleans up on signals, each re-raised so the app stays killable, and readers annotate liveness. O32 there is no port and no server selector, so 'default to the new core' is not expressible as client config — the honest row is an assertion: reads implementation (registry-closed), never serverName (a deployment label the contract forbids discriminating on), never serverBuild.id for equality. Denylist not allowlist so a future registry amendment warns rather than becoming an outage. O33 reply shape only, storage unchanged. Overseer checks before landing: confirmed the owner's live emulator would NOT be falsely refused (his frontend holds /run/user/1000/oracle.sock, on Aurora's default chain; implementation shipped at oracle 0a4313ea 2026-08-25, his process started 2026-08-29), then planted an independent poison making 'cannot tell which server' proceed silently — 3 rows fired naming that verdict, 11 correctly unmoved. Agent's own disclosures kept: its [w1] row went green over a plant because it matched a variable NAME not the mistake, and its O33 wording rows all survived a plant that stopped writing entirely. Merged tree 5848/0/7 (baseline 5817), tsc + build clean, guard checker 170 classified / 0 failures. Parked: O35 the window icon does not render-verify (decode proven, render unmeasurable — no WM under Xvfb); O36 a Wayland detach hypothesis explicitly not measured.

headline: Thirty-six tests could only ever run on your machine, and a wrong folder path made forty-three of them lie about why they failed.
matters: The test suite had your home directory typed into it in three dozen places, so on any other machine those tests could only skip. Worse: if the reference folder was present but empty — a half-finished clone, a wrong path — forty-three tests failed with messages that never mentioned the folder at all, sending the next person to debug a parser or a symbol that was fine. They now say what is actually wrong. A cleanup bug that had been dropping copies of the disassembly into the repo is fixed too.

Two rows used walk-up finders that looked correct and still opened the real tree, caught by an fs-level trace. Also fixed: s1-saveback-roundtrip mkdtemped into the REPO ROOT and restored the api before rmSync, so a failing run left nine untracked un-gitignored copies of the disassembly one `git add -A` from being committed; removal moved to finally. headline: The background repeats before the act ends — and the number everyone was quoting for it, 2,048, was on the wrong axis and was not a wrap width at all.
matters: Backgrounds are meant to repeat sideways; that is how a forest tiles forever, and the editor now just tells you how often, in a tooltip that costs no space. Repeating UP AND DOWN is a tear — sky reappearing below the ground — and until now the editor let you cause one with a single spinner and said nothing until the game ran. It now says so, and only then: it is silent on every background that exists today, and it goes quiet again the moment you take the fix it suggests. A warning you would see on every level is a warning you would learn to ignore.
detail: O21, branch fix/bg-wrap-visibility. THE ARITHMETIC FIRST: 64 is PLANE CELLS, 512 is PLANE PIXELS (the wrap modulus, both axes: BG_WIDTH 64 x TILE_WIDTH_PX 8; aeon PLANE_H_CELLS = PLANE_V_CELLS = 64), 2048 is WORLD PIXELS (SECTION_PIXEL_SIZE, aeon SECTION_SIZE $800). A world px and a plane px are different units and the exchange rate is the parallax factor, per band horizontally and per scene vertically -- so comparing 2048 to 512 is a category error, not an arithmetic one. The row's 2,048 is the VERTICAL OVERSHOOT, traced to this repo's own BG capability survey row 11 (6144 act height - 4096 ceiling at v_factor 3), and it equals SECTION_PIXEL_SIZE BY ACCIDENT, which is why it reads as a wrap width once relayed without its axis. CORRECTION TO THAT SURVEY'S HEADLINE, relayed not edited: it compares act EXTENT; the camera never reaches the last screenful, so the seam-predicting quantity is TRAVEL (5,920) and the figure is 1,824. AGREEMENT, labelled as such rather than dressed as a derivation: Aurora derives travel 5,920 from SECTION_PIXEL_SIZE and SCREEN_HEIGHT alone, and aeon read Camera_Y_Max = 0x1720 = 5920 live off the ROM (d-31). PREMISE: 'wraps 2,048 px' NO; 'before the act ends' YES (aeon witnessed the seam on the running ROM); 'nothing checks it' YES, fully -- aeon's DEFERRED_WORK says no build rule does, and Aurora's renderBg draws the plane once at world origin with no parallax while cameraPreviewPlan only answers at one anchor. BUILT: src/renderer/canvas/bg-wrap.ts (PLANE_COLUMN_SPAN, actReach, bandReach, verticalReach, verticalWrapAdvisory), the fb tooltip readout, the V-factor advisory, aeon.state() now reporting the act grid so a harness derives expectations from the act instead of copying the app's answer. NOT BUILT AND NAMED: canvas marks on the map at each repeat's world position -- the geometry now exists for it. NO LITERAL 512, 2048 OR 5920 IS AN EXPECTATION anywhere: the vitest file spells each figure as the expression producing it and the harness rebuilds the span from the vendored contract plus bg-tiles.ts. RED-FIRST UNDER FOUR PLANTS, including the row's own category error (expected 2048 to be 512) and the advisory-rendered-to-nobody (17/27) -- under which [4h] 'taking the remedy silences it' STAYED GREEN, which is exactly why it is paired with [4a]. headline: The chunk panel told you editing a chunk updates every copy of it. It updates the act you are looking at — so it now says so, and tells you where the others are.
matters: Stamped chunks remember where they came from, and editing the original re-stamps them. That works within one act. A copy in another act kept its link, was never updated, and quietly drifted from the chunk it claimed to remember — while the panel promised otherwise. Making it update everything was not an option: the editor's undo cannot address another act, and across zones the tile numbers mean different things, so it would have corrupted the other act rather than propagating to it. Instead the promise now matches what happens, and after a chunk edit you are told exactly which copies elsewhere were left alone.
detail: O46. Cross-act defect CONFIRMED real: config.chunkLibrary is one project-wide string loaded once into one ChunkDef[], so a copy in another act is the SAME chunk. Three grounds for rejecting cross-act propagation, first two verified by me: (1) NOT EXPRESSIBLE - a command's sectionIndex is a flat index resolved as level.sections[cmd.sectionIndex] against the focused act with per-document undo stacks, so a child meant for act 2 slot 3 writes act 1 slot 3 on undo; (2) across zones a ChunkDef nametable word indexes the ZONE's tileset, so it is corruption not propagation; (3) action at a distance on an unreachable undo step. Chose propagate-in-act plus REPORT, which keeps the capability narrowing alone would have dropped; save toast becomes warning when copies survive, byte-identical when none do. headline: The chunk panel promised that editing a chunk updates every copy. It only ever updated the act you had open. Now it says so, and tells you where the other copies are.

It updated every copy IN THE ACT YOU HAD OPEN — the chunk library is shared by the whole project, so the same chunk stamped in another act quietly kept showing the old art while still claiming to follow the library. Making it reach across acts was rejected for reasons written down in the code: an undo step cannot reach an act you are not looking at, and in another ZONE the same chunk does not even mean the same tiles. So the act you have open still updates, and saving now tells you exactly which other acts still hold un-updated copies and how many, as a warning that stays on screen long enough to read.

FIRST ESTABLISHED THE DEFECT IS REAL rather than assumed: config.chunkLibrary is ONE project-level path -> LoadedS4Config.chunkLibraryPath -> ONE project.chunkLibrary array, while sections hang off zones[].acts[]. Also confirmed art-facet.tsx is the ONLY producer of set-chunk (the agent's save-chunk only ADDS, minting a fresh id), so there is no second propagation path. DESIGN CALL: report, do not propagate. Three grounds, at the head of chunk-links.ts's new section — (1) AnyCommand.sectionIndex is a flat index resolved as level.sections[i] against the FOCUSED act, and undo stacks are per-document (documentHistoryHub.historyFor), so a cross-act child would write the wrong sections on undo; (2) ChunkDef.nametable words are indices into the ZONE tileset (sliceForSave mints them), so cross-zone propagation is corruption; (3) action at a distance in an act the author cannot see. headline: There is now a control for making the background sway — and its 'off' setting is off, which was harder than it sounds.
matters: The engine's numbers for this run backwards in three separate ways: a bigger number means a SMALLER sway, some numbers in the middle of the range are illegal, and 'no sway at all' is the number at the very top rather than zero. A control built the obvious way would have had an off switch that meant maximum. You now pick a sway in pixels from a short list, and a duration in seconds and minutes, and off is its own switch rather than one end of a slider.
detail: EW-7-11 first split, plus the schema re-pin it required. bob_shift is an inverse amplitude (1=128px, 8=1px), domain is exactly {15} union 1..8, and 15 is the no-bob sentinel while the packed wire byte's off is 0. Amplitude is a closed 8-rung select in PIXELS ascending - shift order would leak the inversion back into the place it was being hidden - and the LIST IS THE GUARD rather than a bound, because min/max on a NumberField only style the spinner and never stop a typed value, so a bounded spinner makes 0 unusual not unreachable. Off is a distinct state, not a ninth rung, and OMITS both keys rather than writing 15 (the schema default IS the sentinel; writing it would diff every scene file to restate its silence). Ladder derived from the schema's own anyOf numeric arm, sentinel derived three ways, disjointness asserted at module load. Schema re-vendored by EXTRACTION at empyrean bc639a10: extracted bytes hash to c73d5b42 and are byte-identical to the contract, both re-verified by me. anyOf implemented as anyOf and not as its neighbour oneOf, with an overlap row that fails if the semantics are swapped. 8 poisons all restored, byte-identical round-trip proven on aeon's shipped scene including on-set-off. headline: The test suite refused to run on the main tree whenever finished agent checkouts were lying around. It now steps over them and says so.

headline: A test that was supposed to prove the editor finds its sibling projects correctly was quietly measuring nothing wherever anyone actually ran it; it now builds the conditions it needs and refuses when it cannot.
matters: The check exists because there are two ways to ask git 'where am I', and one of them answers wrongly from a secondary copy of the repo. But the two answers only differ inside such a copy, and the tests normally run in the main one — so the check skipped every ordinary run and had been proving nothing for its whole life. It now creates the copy it needs, measures there, and prints both answers side by side on every run. More importantly, when it cannot tell the two apart it fails saying FIX THE BED, NOT THE RESOLVER — so a future change that quietly breaks the setup gets caught instead of sliding back into a green that means nothing, which is the exact failure this work existed to close.

matters: Ninety-three files each worked out where the editor lives, in two different spellings and two different ways, so pointing a run at another copy moved two thirds of them and quietly left the rest behind. Separately, three tools defaulted to a temporary folder from a session that ended weeks ago; the worst of them is the one whose whole job is to work on a throwaway copy of the engine and never the real one, and its dead default sailed straight past that safety check. It now stops and says what to set. The checker that is supposed to catch this kind of thing could see neither problem, because neither of them mentions a home directory; it can now, and finding out taught it about eight more places.

headline: The editor stopped letting anyone tell it where it lives, and split that question away from the one it was really being asked: which built copy should this run use.
matters: One setting was doing two jobs. It was meant to say which folder the editor lives in — something the code can just look up, and can only be wrong about if someone types it wrong — but it was also the only way to say 'run against the build over there', which is a real need because a second working copy of the repo has no build in it at all. Because the two jobs named the same folder for everyone, nobody could see they were different jobs; the first time somebody used the setting for the second job, it silently moved the whole repo under test. The lookup is now just a lookup, the setting is checked against it and refuses if they disagree, and the second job has its own name. The part that took the longest was how to prove callers were sorted into the right job: a check that the two names AGREE only ever runs where the mistake is invisible, so instead the test points them at different folders on purpose — with the mistake planted, everything else in the suite stays green and only that test goes red.

headline: The harness that borrows another copy's build now says so in a line a test can actually read, instead of one only a running app could print.
matters: When a second working copy of the repo has no build in it, the harness climbs up and uses the nearest copy that does. That is fine — the two are genuinely different things and it is allowed to pick — but only if it tells you which one it picked, because a speed measurement taken against somebody else's build and reported as yours is worthless. It did print that. The problem was where: inside the part of the script that only runs once a real app has launched, so nothing could ever check the wording, and a change that quietly dropped the warning would have looked identical. The message now comes from a small shared piece that a test drives directly against fake folders, and two tests hold it from both sides — one fails if it stops warning, the other fails if it warns every time.

headline: The check that the editor can find the other projects was only ever run in the one situation where it cannot go wrong, so it now runs in the ordinary one too
matters: The editor works out where its neighbouring projects live by asking the version-control tool where its own project folder is. That tool gives a different kind of answer depending on which sort of copy you ask from: from the temporary side copies that helper sessions work in, it always answers with a full address, and from an ordinary everyday copy it answers with a short one that means nothing on its own. Every check we had was written from a side copy, so the short answer had never once been tried, and a version of the editor that got it badly wrong would have looked perfectly healthy in every check we run before merging. A neighbouring project shipped exactly that and only found out after merging. New checks now build a throwaway project of their own, in each of the ordinary shapes, and read the answer back. Each one refuses loudly, in its own words, if the throwaway project it built is not actually capable of telling a right answer from a wrong one, so a check that quietly stops testing anything cannot pass unnoticed. Both were confirmed by deliberately breaking the editor first and watching them go red, and the old checks stayed green through that same break, which is the whole reason the new ones exist.
detail: O74, branch fix/o74-step3-main-checkout, two commits. THE GAP: test/support/sibling-root.mjs step 3 derives the suite root as dirname(dirname(<git rev-parse --git-common-dir>)) with cwd=AURORA_DIR. `git rev-parse --git-common-dir` has THREE output shapes, measured here on git 2.55.0 by the new rows themselves: from a linked worktree an absolute path whether asked or not; from a main-checkout root `.git`; from a main-checkout subdirectory two levels down `../../.git`. The pre-existing step-3 bed is a linked worktree and exercises only the absolute shape; sigil's merged tree went red on the relative one (its mechanism was resolving git's relative output against the process cwd rather than against the directory git ran in — NOT the same mechanism as the mutation below, but the same class of observable). MEASURED BLINDNESS, by the controller before this parcel: with `--path-format=absolute` deleted from our own resolver, the resolver's 38 rows went 38/38 green (the step-3 row asserted only the source-string PREFIX, built from the command name, never from the result; the worktree bed is unaffected; the cwd-pin row asserts stability and non-null, never correctness), the full suite reported ZERO failures at 443 files / 5935 rows against a normal 454 / 6273 because 270 rows became SKIPS not failures (277 skipped against 7), and the literal gate failed for a fabricated reason. Only the announce line named the bug. WHAT LANDED: two rows in test/support/sibling-root.test.ts, `derives the suite root from a MAIN CHECKOUT ROOT, where git answers `.git`` and `derives it from a MAIN-CHECKOUT SUBDIRECTORY, where git answers `../../.git``, sharing makeMainCheckout(nest) / proveStep3FromMainCheckout(). The bed is a scratch `git init` under mkdtemp with the subject COPIED IN at <anchor>/test/support/, since AURORA_DIR is the module's own file location and is what git is handed as cwd; nest=[] gives shape 1 and nest=['packages','editor'] gives shape 3. THE REAL MAIN CHECKOUT WAS DECLINED AS THE BED, deliberately: its expected suite root is exactly what a bed-ignoring resolver answers, so that row cannot discriminate — and these rows run inside a linked worktree half the time anyway. Expectation = dirname(dirname(<absolute --git-common-dir>)) read out of the bed, never typed. FOUR UNMEASURABLE BED REFUSALS before any resolver assertion, following the existing file's refusal shape: (1) git's default answer must be relative — an absolute one means the bed is the linked-worktree case renamed; (2) it must be the shape the row names, so the two rows cannot silently become one; (3) the derivation must differ with and without the flag, else a flag-less resolver passes; (4) the bed's suite root must not equal what the resolver derives from the REAL tree, measured live in the same run by running the real subject — this is the hub's second question answered inside the row. Then the returned step-source (recomputed per call, on stdout, embedding git's cwd) must name the bed's anchor. RED-FIRST TWICE, mutation shown from disk via git diff before each red run. PLANT 1, `--path-format=absolute` deleted from sibling-root.mjs:479 (verified from source that :487 is a purely lexical dirname(dirname(common)) with no resolve(), so a relative common can only yield a relative root): both new rows RED — `expected '.' to be '/tmp/aurora-step3-main-aBBkFL/suite'` and `expected '..' to be '/tmp/aurora-step3-main-0Tzk22/suite'` — and 38 passed, i.e. the linked-worktree row and every other row stayed GREEN, the blindness reproduced in one run. PLANT 2, the inert bed: derive(bed.subject) -> derive() so the row runs the MAIN copy: both rows RED at bed refusal (4)/(5), naming `it derived from /home/volence/sonic_hacks/aurora/.claude/worktrees/agent-... , not from the main checkout /tmp/aurora-step3-main-fsJrW9/suite/aurora this row built`. Both restored with `git checkout HEAD --` from the committed baseline and re-run green. headline: The check now also runs in the copy of the project the code is really checked out as, and says out loud when it could not
matters: The earlier checks each build a throwaway project of their own and read the answer back. That proves the editor can work out where its neighbours live in a project someone assembled for the purpose, and it says nothing about the project the code is actually checked out as, which is where the trouble showed up in a neighbouring team. A further check now asks the question in this copy itself. It was left out at first for a reason that was true but was about a different thing: that check cannot tell whether the editor really looked here or merely gave the right answer from habit, because in this one case the two answers are the same. The reviewer's ruling, and it is right, is that this makes the check narrower rather than empty, and the honest move is to keep it and write the limitation into the check itself, where the next reader will see it, instead of using it as grounds to delete the check. Helper sessions work in a side copy where the situation being checked does not exist, so there it stands down and says in the run's own output that it measured nothing, rather than passing quietly. It was still confirmed by deliberately breaking the editor, in a throwaway ordinary copy assembled for that purpose, and watching it go red.

headline: The written rule that every entry in our work diary must carry a time read off the clock is now checked by the machine, for entries added from today onward
matters: Two of our shared records are meant to be written to and never edited, and each line is supposed to say exactly when it was written, taken from the clock at that moment. Some were not. People typed a time from memory, or rounded it to a tidy number, or filled one in afterwards for something they had done earlier. A measurement built last week showed the difference plainly: lines written properly sit right on top of the moment they were saved, and the others sit minutes or hours away. But it was a tool someone had to remember to run, so nobody did. It now runs with the rest of the checks, every time, and stops the run when a newly added line has a time it could not have read off a clock. The old lines are left exactly as they are. Editing them is forbidden - the whole point of these records is that they are never rewritten - and a check that was red every single day would teach everyone to ignore it. So the new check draws a line at the moment it came into existence: everything older is counted, reported out loud with the reason, and let be; everything from that moment on has to hold up. The line is drawn on when a line was SAVED, not on the date the line claims for itself. That distinction is the whole thing. If it were drawn on the claimed date, then somebody filling in a time for last week's work - one of the two problems this exists to catch - would fall on the old side of the line and never be looked at, and the check would quietly be half blind while appearing to work. Building the proof turned up a real fault in the first version and it is fixed: someone whose bad line had already been shared with the team had no way to put it right, because the old time stayed findable in the history forever and the check stayed red no matter what they did next. Correcting the line now clears it, and the correction itself is held to the same rule, so it cannot be used to slip anything through. Before it was believed, the check was deliberately broken in four different ways and watched to go red each time, including by adding a deliberately wrong line to the diary and taking it out again afterwards - both steps left in the record on purpose, so anyone can see the proof rather than taking my word for it.
detail: O76, branch fix/o76-ledger-timestamp-gate. WHAT LANDED: scripts/check-ledger-timestamps.mjs, fifth in the `npm test` && chain (after check-object-stringify, before check-harness-guards) and also `npm run check:ledger-timestamps`. It shells out to scratchpad/ledger-timestamp-audit.py, which is unchanged in measurement and gains three OPT-IN flags: --since (the ratchet), --strict-ahead, --only-present. WITHOUT THEM the instrument's exit statuses and every finding it prints are identical to master's copy - verified after each method change by running `git show master:` of the file side by side over both ledgers; two message templates gained a sentence naming the new flags and nothing else moved. THE CUTOFF IS ON COMMITTER TIME, NOT ON `at`: IN_FORCE = 2026-09-02T10:22:28Z, read off `date -u` seconds before the commit that added the gate (d39f0fc5, committed 10:22:57Z), so the gate binds its own landing and nothing earlier. It is a pinned constant, not a runtime derivation, because deriving it from the add-commit would move it LATER under any squash or rebase and a cutoff that drifts later grandfathers more; what IS derived is crossCheckInForce(), which reads `git log --diff-filter=A -- <self>` and exits 2 if IN_FORCE is later than it - the landing spot for an edit-it-forward. Today: 135 lane-log + 21 decisions grandfathered, printed with the reason on every run. ELEVEN CANARY CASES run before this repo is judged at all, on `git init` repositories under mkdtemp with GIT_COMMITTER_DATE set, through gateArgs() - the SAME flag list the real run uses, so the canaries cannot drift into testing a different command line. Each names its expected exit status, required substrings and FORBIDDEN substrings; RULES_EXERCISED requires every failure rule to have fired or the run exits 2. THE FIRST CANARY SET LOOKED COMPLETE AND WAS BLIND: every case behaved identically whether the cutoff read the commit or the `at`, so the set would have printed OK with the cutoff moved onto `at`. K4b (committed after the cutoff, `at` claiming before it) is the only discriminator; it asserts '1 entry IN SCOPE' and '1 GRANDFATHERED' as well as the status. RED-FIRST, FOUR MUTATIONS, EACH `git diff`-ed FROM DISK BEFORE ITS RED RUN: (1) in_scope() moved onto `at` -> K4b RED, 'exit 0, expected 1; missing "1 entry IN SCOPE" ... must not contain "0 entries IN SCOPE"', gate exit 2. (2) still_there() -> False, the new method's vacuity risk -> K2 RED, 'missing "1 entry IN SCOPE"', gate exit 2. (3) a lane-log entry planted 20 min adrift and COMMITTED (816c1f90) -> gate exit 1, 'OVER THRESHOLD (1) 1205s 2026-09-02T10:08:52Z', RATCHET line reading 1 entry IN SCOPE / 135 GRANDFATHERED; `npm test` rc=1 with NO 'Test Files' line, i.e. the chain stopped at the gate and vitest never ran. Measured aside: with the same line in the working tree but UNCOMMITTED the gate exits 0, because the audit reads git history - which is why the plant had to be committed. (4) LEDGERS pointed at a tracked-by-nothing path that EXISTS on disk -> audit exit 2, gate exit 2, `npm test` rc=2. (A non-existent path hits the earlier readable guard instead, also exit 2.) All four restored from committed baselines - `git checkout HEAD --`, never on a dirty tree - and re-run green. headline: The second copy of the code that works out where our neighbouring projects live had never been tested at all, and now it is — in both of the situations it has to work in
matters: The editor has to work out where the other projects sitting beside it live on disk. There are two separate pieces of code doing that, one for each of the two programming languages this project is written in, and they have to agree. One of them was thoroughly checked. The other — the one six of our small standalone tools rely on — had no checks whatsoever, in any language, anywhere in the project. That is worse than a check that is wrong, because a wrong check at least shows up somewhere: a piece of code with no checks adds nothing at all to the tally at the end of a run, so a run that never looked at it and a run that looked and found nothing print exactly the same thing. It now has seven checks, and they run every time anyone runs the checks for the whole project. They cover both of the situations that matter: the temporary side copies that helper sessions work in, and the ordinary everyday copy — which give different sorts of answer, and only one of them had ever been tried anywhere in this project until last night. Each check builds its own throwaway project, puts a copy of the code inside it, and then refuses out loud if the throwaway it built is not actually able to tell a right answer from a wrong one, so a check that has quietly stopped testing anything cannot pass unnoticed. Six deliberate breakages were made and each was watched to go red first, including breaking the checks themselves rather than only the code they judge. One real disagreement was found and fixed along the way: the two pieces of code accepted different lists of names for the same setting, so somebody using one of those names got a working answer from one half of the editor and a refusal from the other. Making the two lists match is not the fix — a check that goes red the next time either list changes is, and that is what shipped.
detail: O75, branch fix/o75-python-resolver-tests, three commits. THE GAP, from docs/reviews/2026-09-02-python-twin-untested.md: aurora resolves peer checkouts through two twins, test/support/sibling-root.mjs (rows 106-108) and scratchpad/lib/suite_paths.py, and the Python one had NO test file in any language at any path while 6 instruments import it, so it had a step-3 row in neither configuration. Flattest member of the disjoint-population class four lanes hit on 2026-09-02: the others shipped a green artifact that looked like coverage, this one shipped no artifact, because a module with no test contributes no skip, no failure and no line to any suite total. ARITHMETIC RE-VERIFIED RATHER THAN ASSUMED: _suite_root derives with pathlib.Path(common).parent.parent, which resolves the string against nothing exactly as Node's lexical dirname does, so both twins agree on all three git output shapes ('.git'->'.', '../../.git'->'..', '/a/b/aurora/.git'->'/a/b') and the flag-deletion plant discriminates here for the same reason it does there. WHAT LANDED: scratchpad/lib/test_suite_paths.py, 7 rows, shaped after sibling-root.test.ts's step-3 block rather than invented - a LINKED WORKTREE (the only place --git-common-dir and --show-toplevel disagree), a MAIN-CHECKOUT ROOT ('.git'), a MAIN-CHECKOUT SUBDIRECTORY two levels down ('../../.git'), THIS checkout's own real main checkout (a loud skip naming the production configuration it did not measure, since agent sessions run in a worktree), the CWD PIN that makes copying the subject into each bed the only bed that works, the announce line, and the cross-twin alias comparison. Every bed is CREATED BY THE ROW and the subject is COPIED INTO IT, because _AURORA_DIR_DERIVED is Path(__file__).resolve().parents[2] and is what git is handed as cwd; expectations are mkdtemp paths DERIVED from the bed, asserted to differ both from a flag-less derivation and from what the resolver answers ignoring the bed entirely, the latter MEASURED live in the same run by running the real module. Five bed refusals fire before any resolver assertion and each says FIX THE BED, NOT THE RESOLVER. O73 FOLDED IN AND SETTLED: AEON_ROOT was accepted by the JS twin (sibling-root.mjs checkoutEnvAliases) and refused by the Python one, so one environment resolved for a JS instrument and refused for a Python one; Python accepts it now, but the DELIVERABLE IS THE CROSS-TWIN ROW, which reads both tables live over the JS twin's own SUITE_PEERS plus a non-peer name and compares them IN ORDER, since the first spelling that answers wins. Both files now carry a note where the lists live saying which row will catch the next divergence. RUNNER: scripts/check-python-resolver.mjs, sixth in the `npm test` chain and `npm run check:python-resolver`. python3 -m unittest, NOT pytest - pytest 9.1.1 is installed on this machine and that is exactly the reason not to depend on it; python3 is not a new dependency, since check-ledger-timestamps in this same chain already shells out to a .py and six scratchpad instruments are Python. The gate exists rather than a bare command in package.json because unittest prints `Ran 0 tests ... OK` with exit 0 when discovery matches nothing, which is this parcel's own absence surface one level up: it NAMES the seven rows it requires and exits 2 if any is missing, and prints every skip reason. RED-FIRST, SIX MUTATIONS, EACH `git diff --stat`-ED AND THE LINE QUOTED BACK FROM DISK BEFORE ITS RED RUN: (1) '--path-format=absolute' deleted from _suite_root -> both main-checkout rows RED ("'.' != '/tmp/aurora-py-step3-main-vqjti8md/suite'" and "'..' != '/tmp/aurora-py-step3-main-50v0n2d3/suite'") while the LINKED-WORKTREE ROW STAYED GREEN, the blindness reproduced in one run, and `npm test` rc=1 with ZERO `Test Files` lines, i.e. the chain stopped at the gate and vitest never ran; (2) the main-checkout bed made inert (_probe(bed.subject.parent) -> _probe(SUBJECT.parent)) -> both rows RED at the announce refusal, naming this worktree as the tree actually measured; (2b) the same for the linked-worktree bed -> RED the same way; (3) a required row renamed out of collection -> unittest reports `Ran 6 tests ... OK` and the gate exits 2 naming the absent row; (4a) AEON_ROOT removed from the Python table -> cross-twin row RED; (4b) the JS table REORDERED -> RED naming the first differing element. All restored with `git checkout HEAD --` from a committed baseline and re-run green. The worktree bed's loud-skip path is reachable via AURORA_PY_STEP3_REPO_FOR_TEST and was exercised (=/tmp -> `git worktree add` exit 128, skip printed). NOT DESCRIBED AS ANY OTHER LANE'S BUG, anywhere in the code, the comments, the ROADMAP or here: the sibling defect was resolving git's relative output against the process cwd rather than against the directory git ran in; dropping the flag is a DIFFERENT MECHANISM producing the same class of observable, and the file's header states the fourth reading of a green-under-plant that the distinction exists for. SUITE: 454 files passed / 2 skipped (456), 6275 passed / 8 skipped (6283), zero failures, seven gates exit 0, typecheck clean. THIS PARCEL ADDS NO VITEST ROWS - its seven are counted by the gate, which prints them - so against the controller's main-checkout baseline of 454/2 and 6276/7 the TOTAL IS IDENTICAL (6283) and the one row that moved passed->skipped is row 108's, which skips in a linked worktree and says so. headline: The new checker could report all-clear while the thing it was checking had already been changed on disk, and it can no longer do that
matters: The checks added yesterday for the second half of our project-finding code turned out to have a flaw, not in the checks themselves but in the thing that runs them. To save time, the language they are written in keeps a pre-digested copy of each file and only re-digests it when the file's timestamp or its length changes. So an edit that keeps both — and swapping two words in a list keeps both — leaves the old pre-digested copy in place, and the checks then run against yesterday's version of the file while the changed version sits on disk. The reviewer hit this on his very first attempt at reproducing one of my deliberate breakages: the run came back all-clear, he read it as a fault in my check, and only found the real cause by throwing away the pre-digested copies. My own breakages had happened to avoid the collision, so their results still stand, but the method could have fooled the next person. The runner now hands the language a brand-new empty scratch area for those copies on every run, so nothing left over from any earlier run can be reached, whoever ran what beforehand. Two neater-sounding options were considered and rejected because they only stop new copies being made and do nothing about old ones already lying around, which is exactly the situation this arises in. Proving the fix turned up a second, smaller version of the same fault in my own work: with the fix taken out, the run not only went all-clear over a changed file, it went on printing a line claiming it had read the file fresh. That line was a statement of intent that nothing checked. The runner now counts what the language actually wrote into the scratch area and refuses outright, rather than reporting anything at all, if the count is zero. Both halves were demonstrated by deliberate breakage: with the fix in, the run goes red and names the difference; with it taken out, the identical situation goes all-clear on the version that shipped, and now refuses loudly on the current one.
detail: O75 follow-up, three commits on fix/o75-python-resolver-tests, branch fast-forwarded onto master 99b49066 (the O75 merge) first. RAISED BY THE COORDINATOR AT LANDING, and his verification of the parcel proper is recorded there: in the main checkout all seven rows ran with 0 skipped, the real-main-checkout row ASSERTING rather than skipping, and the flag plant went three-red including AssertionError: '.' != '/home/volence/sonic_hacks' from the real checkout while the linked-worktree row stayed green. THE HOLE: CPython invalidates a cached .pyc on the source's (mtime, size). A mutation preserving BOTH is invisible to it, so the run executes stale bytecode while the changed file sits on disk. This parcel's own alias plants (4 and 4b) are exactly that shape - short edits to a tuple, run seconds apart - and the coordinator hit the FALSE GREEN on his first attempt at the reorder plant, read it as a defect in the cross-twin row, and found the cause only by clearing the cache. My plants happened not to collide, so their results stand; the method could have fooled the next person, which is the thing this parcel exists to end. MEASURED AS A CLEAN A/B ON IDENTICAL DISK STATE, cache first populated the way a human running the rows by hand populates it (`python3 -m unittest discover ...`, which writes scratchpad/lib/__pycache__), then scripts/collide: same-size aeon alias reorder (("LIVE_AEON", "AEON_ROOT") -> ("AEON_ROOT", "LIVE_AEON"), 58 bytes both) plus os.utime back to the original mtime_ns, both re-read from stat and printed as same=True. SHIPPED PRE-FIX GATE, checked out from merge 99b49066: exit 0, `Ran 7 tests ... OK (skipped=1)`, and its own output printed py=['AEON_DIR', 'AURORA_AEON_REPO', 'LIVE_AEON', 'AEON_ROOT'] as fact while grep of the file on disk said ("AEON_ROOT", "LIVE_AEON"). FIXED GATE, same tree, same cache: exit 1, `Lists differ: [... 'AEON_ROOT', 'LIVE_AEON'] != [... 'LIVE_AEON', 'AEON_ROOT'] / First differing element 2`. THE FIX: PYTHONPYCACHEPREFIX pointed at a fresh mkdtemp the gate creates and removes, passed in the child's env so it also governs the processes the rows spawn (the copies of the subject in each bed). NOT -B and NOT PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE, which stop a cache being WRITTEN and do nothing about READING one that already exists - they would leave the hazard armed for everyone who has ever run the rows by hand, which is how the stale cache gets there. Removal registered on `exit` rather than after the run, because die() calls process.exit and a gate that tidies only its happy path litters exactly the runs someone is debugging. A SECOND DEFECT, MINE, FOUND BY PLANTING THE REMOVAL OF THAT FIX: the run went green over the mutation AND WENT ON PRINTING "compiled from source - PYTHONPYCACHEPREFIX was a fresh empty ...", because the sentence was prose about an intention and nothing read anything back. A gate that names the hazard it closed while not closing it is worse than one that says nothing. So the gate now COUNTS the bytecode files Python actually wrote under the prefix (85 on this machine) - the child's own evidence that it compiled there and could reach no earlier cache - and an empty prefix is exit 2, not a caveat. PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE is deleted from the child's env for the same reason: inherited, it would suppress the writes this check reads and turn a real measurement into a false alarm. Third commit moves that refusal AFTER the run's output is printed, because when it fires the rows have usually just printed a confident OK and the two lines together are the whole lesson; refusing first hid the green that is the reason to refuse and read as a crash. RETROACTIVE, since the method changed twice mid-proof: the collision was re-run from the final committed baseline both ways - fix in place -> exit 1 naming the differing element; fix removed -> exit 2, `COULD NOT MEASURE - nothing was compiled under the per-run bytecode prefix ...`, with `Ran 7 tests ... OK (skipped=1)` still visible above it. All restores were `git checkout HEAD --` or `git checkout 99b49066 --` from committed baselines. NOT DONE, and it is the coordinator's call already made: the cross-twin row's docstring gains no note about same-size same-mtime edits, because after this fix the row's plain claim - it fails when either side gains, loses or reorders an alias - is simply true. SUITE: npm test rc=0, 454 files passed / 2 skipped (456), 6275 passed / 8 skipped (6283), seven gates exit 0, typecheck clean; unchanged from the parcel's own landing figures, since this touches only the runner. No emulator was touched.

headline: A hundred and four of our testing tools were asking where their own copy of the project sits when what they needed to know was where the built, runnable copy sits — the same answer at the main desk, a different one in every side workspace
matters: When one of us works on a change, we do it in a side workspace: a second view of the project, sharing its history but holding only the text files. The heavy machinery — the installed parts the program needs to start, and the assembled program itself — lives only at the main copy, because it would be wasteful to duplicate. Our testing tools have to launch the real program to watch it work, so each of them has to answer a question: where is the assembled program? For years they answered it by asking a different question — "which copy of the project am I standing in?" — and then assuming the machinery sat inside it. At the main desk that assumption is right, which is why nobody ever saw the mistake; in a side workspace it points at a program that is not there, and the tool dies with a message about a connection that never appeared, which sounds like a timing problem and is not one. Two days ago we gave the two questions two separate names and converted exactly one tool. This finishes it: a hundred and four tools now ask for the built copy by its own name, and say out loud at the top of every run which copy they measured and whether they had to borrow it from somewhere else — because a number measured against somebody else's build and reported as yours is the failure underneath all of this. Three things are worth saying plainly. First, the count we started from was wrong in both directions, and the way it was wrong is the lesson: eight of the tools could not be seen by the search that defined the job at all — seven work out where they are by a private method that never mentions the shared one, and one sits in a folder the search did not reach. A search that finds nothing and a world with nothing in it produce the same silence. All eight were found afterwards, by the automatic check, not by any search. Second, that automatic check is the part that actually stops this coming back: it now refuses any line that builds a path to the machinery out of the answer to the wrong question, and it runs with every test run, so the next person who writes it the old way is told at once, by line. Third, and this is the honest limit: at the main desk this whole change alters nothing, because both answers name the same folder there. So the tests passing is a check that nothing broke, and it is not evidence that the fix works. The evidence had to come from a real side workspace, and it did: one of the converted tools, run from the workspace this was written in, correctly reported that it was borrowing the main desk's build three folders up, where the old form pointed at two files that are not there.
detail: O72, five commits on fix/o72-built-tree-consumers, cut from master 0bc48156. POPULATION RE-DERIVED, and it disagrees with the brief in both directions. scratchpad/*.mjs at depth 1: 163 files (the brief said 173). Importing AURORA_DIR: 122. Composing a build path off it IN CODE: 104 — one already converted (mapviewport-baseline-harness), so 103 to do, which matches the brief's 107 only after subtracting the 4 files whose only "dist" is prose (distance, distinct, distM); a loose grep counted those. The remaining 18 of the 122 are question 1 and untouched. PLUS EIGHT THE SURVEY COULD NOT SEE: seven derive the checkout from import.meta.url and never name the resolver, so a population defined as "mentions AURORA_DIR" excluded them by construction; and scratchpad/handover/handover-band-harness.mjs is one directory below the *.mjs glob every count in the brief was taken over. All eight found by the new gate rule AFTER the conversion. Total migrated: 104. THE HELPER: scratchpad/lib/run-root.mjs gains electronBin(root), distMain(root), runTarget(here) -> {root,here,borrowed,source,electron,main} and announceRunRoot(run), which writes describeRunRoot to stderr and returns the value. The two artifact paths are now two constants that isRunnableTree also uses, so the predicate that approves a tree and the paths a harness spawns cannot drift. ELECTRON_BIN is read there and only there — 61 files read it before — and it stays out of the resolver's OWNED_ENV on purpose: it names an executable, not a suite checkout. WHAT ROOT STILL MEANS: unchanged. Every migrated file keeps const ROOT = AURORA_DIR for src/ reads, scratchpad/shots-* writes and test/fixtures/ opens — about 135 sites. Only the build paths moved. Rebinding ROOT to the run target (the exemplar's shape) would have sent shot output into the borrowed tree. THE 21 THAT NEEDED A DECISION: six private walks (bg-dangling-ref, bg-tile-picker, s1-nonlevel-families, s1-sonic-preview, composer-priority, chunk-links) climbed for the BINARY only and so could approve a tree with no dist/ and fail one step later; four composed inline at the spawn with no ELECTRON binding; seven derive ROOT from import.meta.url; three import ROOT from canvas-cdp-harness and printed a provenance line naming the wrong tree, one of them reading join(ROOT,'dist','renderer','assets') for real (canvas-cdp now exports MAIN and RUN); one is the handover file. Two vacuous "if (!ELECTRON) throw" guards removed: the old [...].find(existsSync) can be undefined, RUN.electron never is. THE ONE NOT MIGRATED: ozone-x11-proof.mjs drives a synthetic probe app, not Aurora, so a tree with electron and no dist/ is good enough and requiring a build would make it refuse to run on an unbuilt clone. It takes electronBin and keeps its createRequire fallback; a row asserts that, so the exclusion cannot rot into a file resolving nothing. THE GATE: check-peer-path-literals rule 4, checkout-as-build-tree. Rules 1-3 are structurally blind to this class — no home-directory literal, no session scratchpad, no process.env read; the name, the import and the module are all right and only the question is wrong. It is the one FILE-SCOPED rule there, and that is forced: the composition goes through a local alias, so a line-local grep for AURORA_DIR beside an artifact returns ZERO and reads as an empty world. Four alias seeds — the identifier; anything transitively bound to it (a fixpoint, or the second hop reports a clean file); anything bound to an expression over import.meta.url, which is AURORA_DIR hand-rolled and is how seven instruments hid; and by spelling, a binding imported as ROOT, which is how three more did. Five canary lines, two of which must NOT fire: join(ROOT,'scratchpad/shots') is the checkout answering its own question, and ROOT + '/distance-table.json' is why the dist match carries a not-a-word guard. Canary lines are interpolated rather than typed, as rules 2 and 3 already are, so the gate does not fail on its own source — it did, on the first attempt, and exempting the file was the wrong fix because it would have switched rule 4 off for the parts of the gate that legitimately bind const ROOT = AURORA_DIR. RED-FIRST, THREE PLANTS, ONE PER SEED SHAPE, EACH SHOWN ON DISK BEFORE ITS RED RUN: ${ROOT}/dist/main/index.mjs in loop-paint-harness (AURORA_DIR alias), ${ROOT}/node_modules/.bin/electron in priority-lens-harness (import.meta.url-derived ROOT), join(ROOT,'dist','renderer','assets') in art-agent-harness (imported ROOT). Gate exit 1, all three lines named with file and line. Restored with git checkout -- from the committed baseline, re-run exit 0. SIX VITEST ROWS in test/support/run-root.test.ts, all with the two trees pointed apart: the helpers compose off the tree they are GIVEN (checked against a checkout that is a different directory, so a helper reaching for AURORA_DIR cannot pass); ELECTRON_BIN still wins and does not leak into the dist half; THE WORKTREE SHAPE — an unbuilt directory nested under a built one, asserting BOTH that the pre-migration composition names files that are not there and that runTarget names files that are; the announcement actually leaves the process, on stderr and not into stdout; the launcher population is wired, as a set difference rather than a count; and the ozone exception takes electronBin. run() moved from execFileSync to spawnSync for the announcement row — execFileSync surfaces stderr only when the child fails, so that row could not have failed for the right reason. ELECTRON_BIN joined the child-env scrub list. TWO PREDICATE FAILURES RECORDED IN THE FILES THEY BIT, because both are the same shape as the parcel: the first population row asked "names an artifact path in code", which collapses to 11 files AFTER the migration because a migrated harness never spells either path again — a predicate the fix itself invalidates measures the fix, not the property; and its comment stripper was a naive block-comment regex, which found an opening /* inside a // line mentioning src/main/aether/*.ts and deleted that file's run-root import, so the row named the one migrated harness it could not see as the one that had not been migrated. LIVE EVIDENCE FROM A REAL LINKED WORKTREE (this branch's own, which has neither artifact): node scratchpad/band-preset-harness.mjs printed "root: /home/volence/sonic_hacks/aurora BORROWED - this script lives in .../agent-a156100978926c3ae, which has no built app" and "walked up 3 level(s)", then stopped at its own unrelated AEON_DIR refusal. In the same directory the pre-migration composition resolves to two paths existsSync reports false. SUITE: 454 files passed / 2 skipped (456), 6281 passed / 8 skipped (6289), zero failures, seven gates exit 0, typecheck clean. Against the controller's main-checkout baseline of 454/2 and 6276/7 that is +6 passed — exactly the six rows added — and +1 skipped, which is row 108's step-3 row skipping because this run stands in a linked worktree, as it says. GREEN HERE IS A REGRESSION CHECK AND NOT EVIDENCE FOR THE MIGRATION: in the main checkout both names resolve to the same directory, so every harness behaves identically either way. LEFT OPEN: rule 4 does not read .py/.sh (no Python instrument spawns the app today; if one ever does, the row belongs in check-python-resolver.mjs), and the imported-alias seed is a convention keyed on the spelling ROOT — the one seed that could produce a false positive if a module ever exported a run target under that name. cwd: ROOT was left alone at the spawns: it is a valid directory either way and changing it is a behaviour change outside this parcel. No harness was run to completion (none needs to be for this property, and runtime confirmation is the controller's to schedule).

headline: A correction to the entry I wrote twenty minutes ago: the number of tools I changed is a hundred and fourteen, not a hundred and four, and I got it wrong the same way the brief did
matters: The entry above this one says a hundred and four. That was the count as it stood before I had finished — it does not include ten tools I found and fixed later in the same run, and it is off by one more in a way I only saw when I counted the finished work instead of my own notes. This matters more than the arithmetic. The whole point of the entry above is that a search which cannot reach something reports the same silence as a world where that thing does not exist — and the number I published was itself an example: it was my own earlier note, carried forward, not a fresh count of what had actually changed. Nobody checked it because there was nothing to check it against. So: a hundred and fourteen tools changed. A hundred and eleven of them now ask the shared helper directly; the other three get the answer passed along by a tool they already lean on. This entry is added rather than the earlier one edited, because the diary is written to and not rewritten — a record that quietly corrects itself is a record you cannot trust about anything else either.

headline: One of my own new checks passed in my workspace and failed on the shared copy, because it was really asking "does this machine happen to be tidy" — it now asks the project what it contains
matters: The check I added lists every testing tool that starts the program and insists each one asks the shared helper where the built copy is. To get that list it read the folder off the disk. That sounds harmless and is not: it makes the answer depend on what odds and ends a particular machine is carrying rather than on what the project actually contains. Nine such odds and ends sit in that folder on the owner's machine — private tools from earlier sessions, deliberately kept out of the shared history, four of them named one by one in the list of things to leave alone. My workspace is a clean slate and has none of them, so my check went green for me and red for the reviewer, and it would have stayed red on his machine until somebody edited files the project does not own — which nobody could review or undo. The list now comes from the project's own record of what it contains, plus anything brand new that has not been filed yet, which is the moment a check like this most needs to speak. I did not touch the nine. Two smaller things go with it. I checked whether the other new check had the same weakness; it does not, and I proved that rather than reading the code and assuming — by building a fake version of one of those private tools here, with the exact mistake in it, and showing it is passed over, then showing a byte-for-byte copy of it under an ordinary name is caught loudly. Without that second half the first proves nothing, because a harmless fake would also be passed over. And the reviewer noticed my report named a branch that did not exist, which is why his merge failed; the work was all there under the automatic name, and it is now under the right one. That was a checkable fact I stated without checking, in a report otherwise built on measurements, and one of those spoils the credit of the rest.
detail: O72 follow-up, one commit (ca5ab1f2) on fix/o72-built-tree-consumers. RAISED BY THE COORDINATOR AT LANDING; he backed the merge out and master stayed at 0bc48156. THE FAILURE: test/support/run-root.test.ts "every scratchpad instrument that launches the app resolves it through this module" enumerated with readdirSync and went red on the merged tree naming effects-foreground-harness, effects-foreground-2-harness, priority-zoom-probe and short-viewport-harness. All four are named individually in .gitignore (62 and 68 among them); nine such instruments at scratchpad/ depth 1 on the owner's machine, 172 present against 163 tracked. A fresh worktree carries none, so this bed CANNOT structurally exhibit the case and its colour here is not evidence about the main checkout. WHY THE SHAPE WAS WRONG, beyond the four names: a filesystem walk lets whatever debris a machine happens to carry decide the colour - green meant "this checkout has no stray instruments", never "the repo is correct" - and it was red forever on the owner's machine until someone edited untracked files, i.e. pass and fail both decided outside the repo, bar 19's family. A gitignored instrument is deliberately outside the repo's contract; a gate demanding edits to one asks for a change nobody can review or revert. The four were not touched; they are the owner's to judge. THE FIX AND THE ONE DEVIATION, argued rather than made quietly: the row enumerates with git ls-files for tracked PLUS git ls-files --others --exclude-standard for untracked-and-not-ignored. Tracked-only was what was asked for and it fixes the reported defect, but it opens a hole check-peer-path-literals.mjs refuses to open in as many words ("UNTRACKED-BUT-NOT-IGNORED FILES ARE STILL SCANNED, deliberately ... Filtering on 'tracked' instead of 'ignored' would open that hole in the ordinary write-test-commit path"): a brand-new instrument written the old way is untracked at the exact moment its author runs npm test. Two checks policing one population must agree about what that population IS, and them disagreeing about these four files - in the other direction - is the failure being fixed. Dropping the second call is a one-line change if tracked-only is preferred. Loud on unmeasurable: a non-zero git exit throws naming the command rather than yielding an empty list that would render as a clean tree. RULE 4 CHECKED FOR THE SAME DEFECT AND DOES NOT HAVE IT - and it does NOT enumerate tracked files either, which was the question's premise. It walks the filesystem and then drops ONLY what git check-ignore names (scripts/check-peer-path-literals.mjs, the "Drop the files git IGNORES - and only those" block), a third shape, with a measured incident behind it: one harness materialising a vendored peer copy took the run from 1,163 files to 11,688 and the violations from 252 to 5,200. That population - filesystem minus ignored - is exactly what the two git calls above express, which is why the row matches it rather than tracked-only. MEASURED, NOT READ, with a constructed decoy since the real four are absent here: a file written at the ignored path scratchpad/effects-foreground-harness.mjs carrying the pre-migration idiom (git check-ignore -v confirms .gitignore:62) left rule 4 at exit 0 and the fixed row green at 13/13. A BYTE-IDENTICAL COPY at scratchpad/o72-decoy-not-ignored.mjs took rule 4 to exit 1 naming both its lines, and the row to red naming the file. The second half is what makes the first non-vacuous - an inert decoy would leave everything green too - and it doubles as proof the --others call is live, since a tracked-only enumeration would have missed that copy. Both decoys deleted; git status clean before the commit. THE 163 vs 173 RECONCILIATION, now written where the counts live (run-root.mjs's docblock and ROADMAP row 111): 163 is git ls-files at depth 1, 173 was a filesystem walk including the ignored nine and subdirectories. Neither was wrong; neither said which set it counted, which is why the argument was possible at all. BRANCH: my first report named fix/o72-built-tree-consumers and the commits were on the auto-created worktree-agent-a156100978926c3ae, so his merge failed on the name. Renamed with git branch -m (the worktree HEAD follows; the old name is gone rather than duplicated, and git worktree list confirms the checkout is on the new one). Nothing was lost. It was a checkable claim about the tree that I did not check, in a report otherwise built on measurements. SUITE after the fix, from this worktree: 454 files passed / 2 skipped (456), 6281 passed / 8 skipped (6289), npm test exit 0, seven gates green - UNCHANGED from before it, which is expected and is not evidence: this bed carries none of the ignored nine, so the row's behaviour here says nothing about the main checkout. Only a run there settles it.

headline: Two files everything reads at startup had grown until most of what they held was old news; they are now a fifth and a tenth of the size, with nothing thrown away.
matters: The board of yours that shows all six lanes re-reads my status file every half hour, and mine was the second-largest at 24 KB, most of it history of how rows got to where they are. It is now 5 KB. The file a fresh session of mine reads before it can do anything shrank too, though not yet far enough — the rest of that is a job on its own.
detail: Adopting empyrean f4d6d4b (verified ancestor of origin/main): contract/LANE_STATUS.md rule 7 (title <=240 chars, <=20 rows, <=12 KB) and OVERSEER-PROTOCOL.md 'The boot read is bounded' (OVERSEER.md under ~900 lines / 100 KB, dated tails in siblings not read at boot). lane-status.json 24,644 -> 5,439 B: ten non-contract fields holding 14 KB of lane history (bugTierFrozen, retiredAt x5, nextAfterFeature, lostRun, ratified, decisionsTaken) and ten over-bound titles (longest 1,693) moved verbatim to docs/OVERSEER-LOG.md; longest title now 236, 14 rows, all three bounds asserted in the script rather than eyeballed. bugTierFrozen checked for a live ruling before moving: discharged, EW-TIMELINE-EDGE shipped 2026-08-30 per lane-log 08:08:17Z. OVERSEER.md 121,317 -> 113,047 B / 1,238 -> 1,123 lines at commit 0961eb0e, five whole blocks moved with pointers left; losslessness proven by set-difference over every non-blank original line against head+log. RESIDUAL, stated rather than buried: still over both bounds. The remainder is bar precedent narrative plus bar text duplicated from the shared protocol every session already reads at boot -- removable only by rewriting, which is editorial surgery on the boot read and is proposed as its own parcel, not done at speed. TWO CORRECTIONS TO THE RELAY THAT CARRIED THE RULES: the hub said aurora's OVERSEER.md was 'already inside the bound' at 1,238 lines; it is over on both axes, and the protocol's own measurement table (aurora 121 KB) says so. My own first pass at rewritten titles also put two of them over 240; the assert caught it, which is the argument for asserting the bound in the script instead of reading it back.

headline: A booked defect in one of our reference pages had already been fixed an hour and a half after it was written down, and nobody struck it, so it sat for four days pointing at prose that said the opposite
matters: I sent someone to fix two false claims in the page that explains how the editor talks to the rest of the suite. Both had been repaired the same night they were reported — the report was written at 20:34 and the fix landed at 22:10 — but the queue row was never closed, so it stood for four days telling every reader to go fix something already fixed. The real defect turned out to be underneath: that page points at the engine's source by line number, and six of the eight line numbers had drifted in four days. Every claim was still true; only the coordinates had rotted, which is precisely why a bare line number is not worth much on its own — nothing tells you when it stops being right. So the fix is not the new numbers, it is a note at the top naming the exact engine revision the numbers were checked against, scoped honestly to the two paragraphs that were checked and explicitly disclaiming the rest of the page. One claim also got stronger rather than merely renumbered: the page used to say every section carries the default background setting, which is a count that goes stale the moment someone adds a section; it now says the constructor they all go through has no background parameter at all, so no section can carry anything else. Two things worth your knowing. The person doing the work caught themselves inventing a section heading that does not exist in the page, and fixed it before committing — which would have been the same bug one layer up, in a fix for that bug. And they widened scope by one item without being asked, correctly: a third stale claim sat inside a sentence they were already correcting and would have read as self-contradictory next to it. They flagged it rather than doing it quietly, and I checked it and accepted it.
detail: R100 / ROADMAP row 100. Branch fix/r100-mcp-doc-staleness, commit 193185be, merge 368c3f11, pushed (ls-remote confirms origin/master moved, not the push's own output). headline: The effects panel told you variant and cycle controls were not supported by the engine yet; the engine now supports them, so that sentence is gone from the screen
matters: When we built the variant and cycle controls, the engine could not yet consume them, so the panel carried an honest warning saying so. The engine half landed today, so the warning had become a lie and it is now removed — confirmed by driving the real app and checking that no element on that section still shows the sentence, not by reading the code and assuming. The interesting part is how we found out. A check we wrote earlier was designed to go red on exactly this event and to say in its own failure message what to do about it, and that is precisely what happened; nobody had to notice. Two things I want to be straight about. First, the engine work is MERGED but the paired certification run went red, so what I can honestly say is that the code is in, not that the ROM has been proven to do it. If the next certification run differs from the last, the sentence comes back — that condition is written into the code and the roadmap rather than living in anyone's head. Second, I told the person doing this to delete the now-red check, and they refused and were right: they measured what would happen if the engine work were reverted and found every remaining check would have stayed green, so deleting it would have left us quieter rather than safer. They re-aimed it instead, so it now watches for the opposite problem, and they proved it fires in both directions.
detail: R97-LAG. Branch fix/retire-preset-lag-disclosure, commits fd04170c + b1f00c75, merge 91a76d12, pushed (ls-remote confirms origin/master moved). Premise verified by me at aeon a5e2b618 (ancestor of origin/master): tools/effects_gen.py PRESET_KEYS carries cycles+variants at :280, _check_cycles/:670 and _check_variants/:718 shape-check them, render_cycle_channel/:1267 and render_variant/:1316 lower them, and the committed generated effects_scenes.emp carries a real pal_variant — engine support, not a doc heading. TWO reds, TWO causes: the lag row discharged as designed; the 'agrees on every shape' row was a separate latent defect — it compared aeon's ACCEPTED set against the schema's REQUIRED set, equal only by coincidence while the two optional keys were refused, wrong in general since the 12aecd5 re-vendor. Peer-unreachable proven: all three aeon rows ctx.skip loudly. Suite on the MERGED tree, measured by me: 6284 passed / 0 failed / 7 skipped in 456 files. FOREGROUND ITEM DISCHARGED (agent could not run it): npm run harness:variant-cycle 31/31 exit 0, twice, on a FRESH copy per run materialised via git archive from aeon a5e2b618 (never the live tree — aeon is mid-freeze); row [2f] confirms no element on the open section carries the lead sentence; dpr 1, 1680x1050 printed beside the number; teardown ORDERED, SIGKILLed 0.
