headline: A booked defect turned out to be a quarter the size we thought, and the piece that was left had one cause nobody had named: a check that was correct about the wrong list
matters: A note in our queue said that opening a half-complete copy of the Sonic 1 project broke 27 files' worth of checks with unhelpful errors. That number was written before an earlier fix and nobody had re-measured it. Measured properly — by building a complete copy and then removing one file at a time, 46 times, running everything after each — the earlier fix had already handled 88 percent of it. What was actually left was nine checks. Those nine had one shared cause worth understanding, because it is the kind of thing that survives careful review. There is a flag on each required file saying 'if this is missing, the act that owns it is unavailable'. The shared collision tables belong to no single act, so the flag is set to false, and that is CORRECT. The consequence is that the program went on truthfully reporting all eighteen acts as available while every one of them threw the moment it tried to read those tables. One missing file broke 33 checks, eight of them straight through a guard that had just answered honestly about the wrong list. The guard was right; it was answering a question next to the one that mattered. You cannot find that by breaking things on purpose to see if the guard notices, because the guard never looks at the thing in question. Two things about how the measuring went, since the numbers are only worth what the method is. The person doing it caught themselves contaminating their own sweep — the later cases ran while the fix was being written into the same folder, and one of them reported an improvement that does not exist. They threw those away and re-ran all of them from a clean copy, and every number above comes from the clean set. And they reported their leftover failures as 'pre-existing and unrelated', which was true when they started and had stopped being true by the time they finished, because I had merged the fix for exactly those while they worked. On the combined result there are none.
detail: O45 -> ROADMAP row 112. Branch fix/o45-partial-checkout-file-guards, 4 commits (996b6be5, cc7d4c6d, 5e0a7eb2, 0a6f28e8), merge 601fd7bb, tip 89c709d3, pushed with ls-remote confirming. PHASE 1, both states printed: state 1 'no checkout' (EMPYREAN_SUITE_ROOT=$(mktemp -d)) 0 failed / 5950 passed / 278 skipped, O39's territory clean. State 2 'real checkout missing ONE file', complete copy at s1disasm f6ece657 (970 files) reproducing the live run exactly, 46 files removed one at a time: 243 new failing rows — NAMED 152 (63%), ANCHOR 61 (25%), MISDIRECT 28 (11.5%), NAMES-FILE-ONLY 2 (0.8%). Real scope 9 rows in 7 files, not 27 files / 135 tests; the booked figure predated O39 and is retired. CAUSE: ProfileEntry.gating means 'a miss makes the OWNING ACT unavailable'; shared collision tables have no owning act so gating:false is correct, availability truthfully reports 18/18 available while read() throws for all 18, and every O39 guard derives act inputs by filtering on zone/act so a global entry matches no act. collide/Angle Map.bin: 33 rows, 8 through whenS1Act. Aurora bar 2b (wrong observable) on a guard passing every other bar, unreachable by planting. AFTER: MISDIRECT 28->0, NAMES-FILE-ONLY 2->0, NAMED 96->96, ANCHOR 23->23, 0 failed->passed, 0 failed->gone, 0 new. Red-first with mutations quoted from disk, restored from committed HEAD: 7 passed -> M1 3 failed -> M2 1 -> M3 2 -> M4 1 -> restored 7 passed; M1's console.log printed the mutated text, proving the patched file executed rather than a cache. The load-bearing row DROPS each global entry in turn and asserts the measured set equals S1_GLOBAL_REQUIRED_KEYS, and prints the artifact it judges. Peer unreachable: 0 failed. Peer ../s1disasm byte-for-byte unchanged. Merged-tree suite measured by me: 6291 passed / 0 failed / 7 skipped in 457 files. AGENT SELF-CORRECTIONS RATIFIED: (1) contaminated sweep cases 30-46 re-run from detached HEAD at the branch point, one phantom 71-row shrink discarded; (2) a matcher reported 11 rows 'gone quiet' because a beforeAll throw reports at describe level while skips are per-it — resolved to 0. STATED LIMIT: read-tracing shim is a LOWER BOUND, blind to named `import { readFileSync } from 'fs'`; 46 of 178 read paths sampled, 132 not individually removed; not an exhaustive sweep. MY CORRECTION TO ITS REPORT: its 2 'pre-existing and unrelated' failures were the effects-preset drift rows whose fix I merged mid-parcel; zero on the merged tree. ALSO: its archive line read `state: done`, an enum absent from contract/LANE_STATUS.md and one copy-paste from blanking the owner's card; corrected in docs/OVERSEER-LOG.md with the reason. BOOKED, NOT CLAIMED: three shipped error strings in src/core/project/s1/index.ts are driven by no UI test — unit-proven, unproven on screen.

headline: The third queue row in a row turned out to be already fixed — this one by the engine lane, four days ago, and nobody told the queue
matters: A note said the editor's background library was half-committed: the project records WHICH background a section uses, but the picture itself was excluded from the repository, so anyone with a fresh copy got a project pointing at an image they did not have, and the editor quietly fell back to a default. The note left it to me to decide between committing the pictures or declaring them local to your machine. The decision had already been made and shipped by the engine lane the day after the note was written: they commit the pictures. I confirmed it by looking at what is actually in the repository rather than by reading their report — all 34 background files are there, and none is excluded any more. One part is worth more than the fix. They did it in two steps, and the second is what makes it last: the first step named the one background in use, which would have left the NEXT background you author excluded all over again; the second replaced that with a rule covering the whole family. I checked that our own save path writes names that rule actually catches, because a fix that covers today's files and not tomorrow's would look identical from here. It does. So: nothing for me to build, and the note is struck. But that is now three rows in one session that were finished before I got to them, and in each case the only thing missing was somebody closing the row. I am treating that as the finding rather than as three coincidences.
detail: R101 / ROADMAP row 101, struck. NO Aurora code change. Resolved at aeon 838f3129 (2026-08-30, 'fix: track the background the project actually names'), one day after the row was booked 2026-08-29. Verified here at aeon origin/master BY ARTIFACT: `ls-tree -r --name-only origin/master` shows 34 ojz_bg_*.bin blobs including both files the row names (ojz_bg_ingame-forest-v15-1786630615596.bin blob 99e7b601, _tiles.bin blob 28daa612); `git status --porcelain --ignored=matching` reports ZERO ojz_bg bins as '!!'. DURABILITY CHECKED SEPARATELY, because 34 force-adds under a surviving ignore rule would look identical at the tip: .gitignore:140-141 is the NARROW negation from 838f3129 (deliberately scoped, parking the 16 deep-forest experiments as the owner's call), and .gitignore:18 `!games/sonic4/data/editor/ojz_bg_*.bin` is a later BLANKET negation for the family. Aurora writes editor/${zoneId}_bg_${id}.bin and ${zoneId}_bg_${id}_tiles.bin (src/core/formats/bg-library.ts:21-27), both matched by line 18, so the next authored background is re-included with no .gitignore edit. METHOD NOTE: `git check-ignore -v` returned exit 0 while showing a NEGATION rule, which is ambiguous about the actual verdict; I did not assert from it and used `status --ignored=matching` instead, which answers the question directly. Two other false-zero shapes hit and corrected the same hour: `bc` absent (sum via awk) and an `ls` that returned empty through the eza alias. PATTERN, third instance this session: row 100 fixed 1h36m after booking, row 101 fixed ~1 day after booking, O45's figure (27 files/135 tests) stale by 3x after O39. Each closed by someone who did not strike the row.

headline: The file every fresh session of mine has to read before it can do anything is a tenth smaller and back inside the suite limit, with nothing thrown away
matters: Each time one of my sessions starts, it reads a single briefing file end to end before it can do useful work. That file had grown to 110 KB against a suite limit of about 100, so every start paid for every night that came before it. It is now 97 KB and inside the limit, and not one sentence was deleted — five closed episodes moved verbatim into a companion file nothing reads at startup, each leaving behind the rule it taught. The care here is all in one place: the difference between a closed story and a live rule. A story about how we discovered something can go; the instruction it produced must stay, because a rule that quietly vanishes is worse than a file that is slightly too big. I named fourteen rules that had to survive before the work started, and checked all fourteen afterwards against the finished file rather than trusting the report. It is still 141 lines over the line half of the limit. I stopped there deliberately. Getting under it means rewriting live rulings that are tangled up with the stories around them, and the suite's own rule says that is your call, not a lane's tidy-up. I would rather hand you a file slightly over the line count with every ruling intact than one that hits the number with a ruling missing.
detail: Branch docs/boot-read-bound, commit 70b47c5c, merge 4c3a2f1 (see tip). BEFORE 1,173 lines / 110,411 B; AFTER 1,041 / 97,897 — 2,103 B UNDER the byte bound, 141 lines OVER the line bound. LOG 415 -> 706 lines / 44,955 -> 71,137 B, pure append (@@ -413,3 +413,294 @@), nothing reordered. Five blocks moved as protocol move (2): initialize build-identity (65->25), resume/stop race (55->30), built-binary enumeration parameter (28->10), BgAnim driver (46->22), pinned-checkout-vs-pinned-build (53->32). Move (1) NOT redone — a prior measurement found 3 of 125 lines under the nine 'duplicate' bars were verbatim protocol, so pointer-ising would delete local precedent. No bar touched; the CROSS-REPO GREP section and the BEFORE BUILDING AEON procedure row untouched. LOSSLESSNESS re-run by me, not taken on report: set-difference of every non-blank original line against head+log = 0 in NEITHER file. MUST-SURVIVE re-verified by me: all 14 named rules present in the merged head. METHOD FAILURES, MINE, both caught before they became a wrong verdict: (1) a first pass grepped multi-word phrases against a WRAPPED file and reported two rulings LOST that were present, split across line breaks — normalising whitespace fixed it; (2) the retry used an UNQUOTED heredoc, so zsh substituted the backticked patterns: 'never `serverName`' degraded to 'never ' and matched TRIVIALLY (a false POSITIVE on a rule I was trying to confirm) while '`run_to`' was stripped into a false negative. Quoted heredoc, then all 14 verified. Both are the false-zero family, and the false-positive direction is the more dangerous one because it confirms what you hoped. AGENT FLAGGED FOUR LIVE RULES I HAD NOT NAMED and kept rather than moved them (the safe direction), reported per the escape hatch: oracle's 'when a check looks redundant, ask what each of the two claims is before collapsing them'; run_to's reached == predicate_fired being a live claim about OUR code plus the hosted-path citation limit; the bg_anim.emp:103 comment warning and its open action to tell the hub on a fourth instance; and aeon's always-dirty main tree. Ratified, all four kept. It also moved sigil's not-relinking-during-the-freeze state to the log, correctly noting the very next row says never to snapshot another lane's live state here.

headline: Twenty-eight of our tests have their pass-or-fail decided by another person's half-finished edits, and we now know exactly which, because three cheaper ways of finding out would each have answered 'none'
matters: Every sibling project on this machine is somebody's live working copy, so a test that reads one is really asking 'what is in that person's folder right now'. The question was which of our tests actually depend on the CONTENT rather than merely naming a path. The answer is 28 of 56, and the file areas behind them are now listed. The way that number was obtained is the valuable part. Searching the text finds where a file is READ but never whether anything is CHECKED against it. Intercepting the file-reading machinery — the obvious approach — silently does not work under our test runner, and would have printed a confident 'none exposed'. A third tool is not installed. So the method used instead was to copy the neighbouring project, deliberately corrupt the copy in two different ways, and see which of our tests changed colour. That touches nothing of theirs and it measures the thing we actually care about. It also corrected the note that started this. The note said two specific art files were being read by our tests. They are named by them, but nothing checks their contents — proven by putting the original bytes back and watching nothing move, and then, because 'nothing moved' is also what a broken experiment looks like, by swapping those two files' contents with each other as a positive control. The impression almost certainly came from a neighbouring test that reads a DIFFERENT file with a very similar name. One decision needed me. The natural fix is to copy the neighbour's files into our own project so our tests stop depending on their desk. For almost everything that is right and cheap. For one folder it would be actively harmful: two of our checks exist to ask whether that neighbour has since grown a fifth thing of a certain kind, and a frozen copy would contain exactly four forever and would answer 'no' every time it is ever run. So that folder stays live and gets a different kind of check instead. Copying it would have looked tidier and quietly destroyed the only thing those two checks are for.
detail: Row 78 phase 1. Branch fix/row78-s1disasm-live-tree, commits e755aea9 + fc6363e5, merge afd21e75, pushed. Instrument scripts/classify-peer-tree-reads.mjs (committed, prints its own table): A=28, C=6, B=2, D=20 over 56 files; 84 files name the peer. Two independent invocations identical; 'base' run twice as control. Method: perturb a COPY and watch the colour (swap = same-extension rotation, realistic; scram = same-length noise, destructive, deliberately second; empty; plus 35 per-subtree runs for attribution). Three cheaper instruments rejected ON MEASUREMENT, not by argument: grep finds the read never the assert; an fs monkeypatch reports NAMED_SEEN=0 under vitest because Node's ESM facade snapshots the named export and this tree uses `import { readFileSync }` — a confident empty class A; strace absent. Class-A backing subtrees: _maps 12, _anim 5, artnem 5, levels 4, artunc 4, map16 3, objpos 3, map256/startpos 2, collide/palette/sonic.asm/_incObj/_Constants.asm 1 each. headline: Our tests no longer depend on what is sitting unsaved in somebody else's folder — except for two questions that have to, and those now say so out loud
matters: Twenty-eight of our tests were reading a neighbouring project's live working copy, so their pass or fail was decided by whatever that person had half-finished at the time. Those now read a frozen copy kept inside our own project — 595 files, about one megabyte, smaller than the test material we already carry — recorded with the exact revision it came from and a re-fetch recipe. The proof it worked is that the whole suite still passes with the neighbouring project made completely unreachable. If it were still reading their folder, it could not. One folder was deliberately left reading their live copy, and this is the part I want on record because the tidy answer was the wrong one. Two of our checks exist to ask whether that neighbour has since grown a fifth thing of a certain kind. Freezing a copy would make those checks contain exactly four forever and answer 'no' every time they ever run — passing, permanently, while detecting nothing. That was not argued, it was measured: against a copy where a fifth one really had been added, asking the live source finds it and asking the frozen copy does not. So those two questions keep reading the neighbour, and when the neighbour is missing they now announce 'SKIPPED, NOT PASSED — cannot measure', instead of quietly counting as a pass. Two smaller things worth knowing. The person doing this poisoned their own new check and found it broken — not the check itself, but the message it printed on failure, which showed a wall of text naming no file and no revision, so a real failure would have told a reader nothing. And they added 75 files beyond what I authorised, which I have accepted: without them two of our loudest checks go red, and no amount of analysis could have predicted that, only trying it.

ITS PLANT 3 FOUND A REAL DEFECT IN ITS OWN GATE (invariant 8c): the STALE EXEMPTION check fires precisely when a path is untracked, and the rule keyed on tracked paths, so the check written to stop the exemption list rotting was structurally unable to fail - it printed and did not gate. So the rule reaches nested paths and all three suffixes - its regex is /-(harness|probe|proof)\.mjs$/ read from source. headline: A background band can now move UP instead of only sideways - the thing you asked for on 27 August. And aeon's safety net for it turns out to have a hole, which I proved rather than argued.
matters: Until tonight every animated background could only scroll horizontally. The editor now lets you pick the direction, and the wrong pick is refused instead of quietly shipping a background that shimmers in place.
detail: EW-BAND-AXIS / DoD item 8, Aurora's half. Branch feat/ew-band-axis-vertical, 4 commits, merge on master, tip 1ed3b32a, pushed (remote confirmed by ls-remote). Aeon's engine half was chain 210 cc4cded2, contract read at 3a4712fa via git show, never through their working path. 27 new rows across test/formats/bg-anim-band-axis{,-aeon-gate}.test.ts; suite 6436 -> 6468 passing, 0 failing, tsc clean, VERIFIED BY ME ON THE MERGED TREE not branch-side. THE THREE WRITER OBLIGATIONS aeon says the consumer CANNOT check: (1) slot order - one bandCellSlot/bandSlotCell pair now used by all four grid readers, asserted at named POSITIONS because set/count/checksum are vacuous here by construction; (2) phases translate along the declared axis - whole-pixel-plane assertions on both arms plus the converse; (3) axis survives a round trip, never injected when absent. Red-first per plant: slot-order 20/27 red, phase-axis 2/27, pre-parcel-writer 4/27, round-trip 13/27, period 14/27, unit 4/27, each mutation quoted from its own git diff -U0 and restored from a committed baseline. ROW 55's CAUTION WAS WRONG AND IS RECORDED AS WRONG: it guessed the power-of-two constraint would change shape; it does not - col_shift is log2 of the rotation UNIT and step_mask the period, so the vertical arm reuses the same DMA rotate with no engine byte moved; what moves is WHICH KEY carries the rule (rows horizontal, cols vertical). MY OWN FINDING, independently reproduced from the agent's disclosure and the reason I am not treating this as closed: AEON'S GUARD HAS A REACHABLE HOLE. validate_band_phase_axis decodes every bank COLUMN-MAJOR unconditionally, so on a row-major band it reads a permutation of the real picture, the true x-roll stops looking like an x-roll, and it admits. Measured against their real function at 3a4712fa with a no-symmetry fixture ((x*7+y*13)%15+1), phases as exact x-rolls, axis vertical, changing ONLY the slot order: column-major REFUSED (my control, proving the fixture is well-formed and the guard reachable), row-major ADMITTED - the shimmer ships. Their _band_pixels docstring argues 'a consistent relabelling of the slots cannot turn a non-translation into one', which is TRUE AND ABOUT THE WRONG DIRECTION: it rules out false positives while the exposure is a false negative. Their contract 1.2 conditions the refusal on the PHASES alone, so it promises a check strictly broader than the code. Relayed to aeon with both remedies and my recommendation (narrow the contract text now, decode by declared axis when a vertical band actually exists); their population is empty today so nothing ships broken. Aurora can no longer produce the shape at all - the axis is read off the band, so the horizontal arm cannot be asked for on a vertical one. AGENT DISCLOSED ITS OWN NON-DISCRIMINATING ROW (the anti-vacuous control's set/count/sum assertions rule out nothing; only its trailing not.toEqual discriminates) - eighth parcel running to disclose one. RETIRED RULE FOUND IN NINE LIVE SITES, not the two expected; the drift gate now asserts the old sentence is GONE rather than that a new one is present. VENDORED CONTRACT IS A DERIVATION NOT A BLOB COPY (its gate hashes our text) - updated as source with an amendments record rather than hand-edited to match a diff. BLOCKED AND REPORTED, NOT WORKED AROUND: no ROM built, SIGIL_BUILD/SIGIL_EMIT unset in the worktree and a build would have required writing into ../aeon. STILL OPEN AND MINE: the on-screen proof, headless against a private emulator - VRAM tile bytes at the band's own slots against a control run of blob slots the band does not own, since a screenshot diff cannot separate stepping from scrolling. Also open, not introduced here: Aurora's promote door cannot place a band as a rectangle (it inherits the layout's existing cell-to-tile mapping), so obligation 1 is enforced over Aurora's readers rather than the author's picture.

headline: A background you set to move UP actually moves up in the game - built into a real ROM, run, and measured. That is the whole feature working end to end.
matters: Yesterday a background could only ever scroll sideways. You can now pick the direction in the editor and the game obeys it. Nobody has looked at it on a screen yet - that part is yours.
detail: EW-AXIS-ONSCREEN, closing the runtime half of DoD item 8. Packet docs/reviews/2026-09-03-vertical-band-onscreen-proof.md; authoring script + its runner committed so it reproduces. Merge tip after push. FOUR LINKS, EACH MEASURED SEPARATELY because one green at the end would not say which held. (1) AUTHORED THROUGH AURORA'S OWN CODEC, not hand JSON: parseBgOverride -> axis vertical -> shiftedPhaseBanks -> serializeBgOverride on the act's real editor_bg_override.json; pattern_px from bandPatternPx, never typed. ITS ANTI-VACUOUS ROWS ARE THE REASON THE REST MEANS ANYTHING: a band uniform along an axis is a vertical roll AND a horizontal roll at once, which aeon admits as ambiguous and which would satisfy every later assertion while proving nothing about direction - so the script refuses unless phase 0 varies along BOTH axes, then asserts both directions (bank 1 IS a Y-roll, is NOT an X-roll). (2) AEON'S OWN GUARD validate_band_phase_axis ADMITS it, called from a pinned copy. (3) THE GENERATOR LOWERS IT AS VERTICAL: hdr [2, 2, 31, 8, 32, $8000] - step_mask 31 = rows*8-1 (period along Y), col_shift 8 so the rotation unit is 1<<8 = 256 = cols*32, a whole tile row; the same band declared horizontal lowers to 63 and 7. Both derived from cols=8 rows=4, not copied. Generator's own comment: 'vertical (scrolls up)'. (4) IT STEPS IN THE RUNNING MACHINE: band VRAM 0x8000 (the $8000 in the emitted header, so the address came from the artifact) shows THREE DISTINCT CONTENTS at frames 600/640/680 while the control block at 0x8400 is BYTE-IDENTICAL at all three. A screenshot diff cannot answer this - a band DMAs new pixels into fixed slots so the picture differs whether or not it steps; VRAM bytes against a control is the standing bar here since 2026-08-27. headline: The timestamp check told you how to fix a bad entry, and for the commonest mistake that advice did not work.
matters: When two log entries accidentally get stamped with the same second, the check goes red and prints one instruction: correct the entry. Following it changed nothing — the run stayed red whichever of the two you corrected, because the check was watching the shared second rather than the offending line, and the innocent entry kept that second forever. The only escape was editing both, which nothing ever said. That is exactly what happened here last night and it had to be worked out by hand under a red suite. Now correcting the later entry clears it, and the check says which one to correct and which correction will not help.
detail: O57. The duplicate record in ledger-timestamp-audit.py's collect() carried no `raw`, so still_there() fell through to keying it on the stamp instead of on the line; unparsed lines already keyed on the line. Adding the field routes it down that branch. The two directions are deliberately asymmetric: correcting the LATER appearance clears the run and is reported as withdrawn (counted and printed, never dropped); correcting the FIRST does not and must not, because the later entry is still in the file and was still never judged. Six canaries in the gate (K6d correct-the-second clears, K6e correct-the-first does not, K6f a correction that is itself remembered still fails at its own commit, K6g the innocent pre-cutoff re-add stays green, K6h/K6i pin the rejected mechanism). Open call taken: key on the raw line, not on a count of occurrences at HEAD. The agent built the counting variant and ran both over the same beds rather than arguing the edges — they differ on exactly two cases: counting handles two byte-identical appearances where set-keying errs RED (a stuck failure that announces itself), and counting goes SILENTLY GREEN when a colliding line is removed and re-added verbatim with nothing corrected, which is the dominant innocent commit pattern the audit's own header opens with. The limit is written into the LIMITS section and pinned by K6i. Its own first written justification named three edges and one of them (a reorder) was measured wrong; d81b42c4 replaced the guesses with the measurement. Also found: K6's comment credited its innocent half to "K1's repo", which has one commit and performs no re-add, so nothing had ever measured it until K6g — an assertion standing in for a case, inside the file whose whole argument is that those differ. Verified by the overseer rather than taken on report: dropping the raw field puts K6d red with the mutation quoted off disk; an independently written symmetric mechanism (clear once one line with that stamp survives) puts K6e red, so the asymmetry is not vacuous; the bare instrument with no flags is byte-identical on both ledgers before and after, same exit; the real-ledger verdict is unmoved and the grandfathered counts untouched, the only content changes being the canary/rule totals and the new withdrawn-collision line. Scope ruled: the 8 pre-cutoff repeated stamps in lane-log and 4 in decisions stay grandfathered — the ratchet spares them by design and the ledgers are not rewritten. headline: A test rig that passed every one of its 44 checks was reporting FAILED to anything reading it automatically - and the reason was that it deleted a file belonging to the thing that launched it.
matters: This is why an automated sweep of the test rigs could not be trusted. The rig itself was always honest: run it by hand and it says 44 passed and reports success. But when something wraps it - which is what a sweep does - the rig tore down by deleting a temporary folder it thought was its own. It was not: it belonged to the wrapper outside it, and the rig had inherited the path without noticing. The wrapper then tripped over the missing file and reported failure, long after the rig had already reported success. It is the same mistake the code already warned about for a neighbouring setting, one field over, where nobody thought to apply it. The claim attached to this bug - that it had mis-scored 101 results - turned out to be a different number entirely: 101 is how many rigs could not be run by name at all, borrowed and reused. The real count in that same record is two.

headline: Master is green again - and picking up the new effects contract exposed that the editor had quietly stopped rejecting unknown keys in a whole document.
matters: The red was never ours: the shared contract was republished and our freshness check noticed, which is exactly its job. Taking the new version in is routine. What is not routine is what the work found next door. The editor is supposed to refuse a document containing a key it does not recognise - that is what stops a typo silently becoming a setting nobody applies. Because of how the new contract is shaped, that refusal was being skipped for the ENTIRE document. It had been broken in a smaller corner since August and was invisible, because a different check happens to catch most cases first; the new shape is what dragged it into the light. Also worth knowing: the new setting can be written in a way that reads perfectly and is wrong by a whole pixel, with every number inside its allowed range so nothing can catch it. That one is now a named test that explains itself when it fails.

headline: You can now author the new smooth-scroll effect in the panel - five fields, no curve editor, and switching a preset to it is genuinely one undo away.
matters: This is the last unbuilt half of that effect: the engine can do it, the file format carries it, and now there is somewhere to type it. Three things I think are worth your attention. First, the readout shows you BOTH numbers - the lines the effect writes on, and the lines it actually appears on, which are one apart because of how the hardware works. Getting that wrong would have looked completely correct on screen while being one line off everywhere. Second, a rate you might reasonably type - minus a half pixel - simply cannot be expressed in this format at all. Rather than quietly rounding it to something else, it refuses and tells you the two nearest rates you CAN have. Third, and because you have two open questions from me today about controls that cannot be undone: switching a preset between the two kinds throws the other one away, so I made being properly undoable a condition of building it at all. It was measured in the running app - switch, one undo, and the document is byte-for-byte what it was.

headline: We went looking for a test rig that fails 44% of the time, could not make it fail once in nine tries, and found two worse things on the way - one of which made whole runs report success after doing less than half their work.
matters: The honest headline is the negative one, and it is reported as a negative: the fault did not reproduce, and no improvement is claimed. Nine clean runs in a row would happen about once in a hundred times if the old rate still held, so something has changed and nobody knows what - that is written down rather than smoothed into a fix. What the work is actually worth is two things it found instead. First, every session in that rig now PROVES its data reached disk, where before thirty-six of them passed without anyone checking that at all. Second, and this is the serious one: if a browser tab died mid-question, the rig would quietly stop about 45% of the way through and exit reporting SUCCESS, with no summary. Any automated sweep reading that would have recorded a pass for a run that never finished. That is the same class of bug as the one fixed this afternoon, from the opposite side - and it is now closed twice over, so a run that ends without a summary cannot report success by any route.
detail: Merge 93c94c58, pushed. BEFORE: 0 trips in 9 runs of the UNTOUCHED master instrument (load 1.54-10.70, uptime 9d 7:29-7:52) against O50's measured 44%; nine consecutive cleans at that rate is ~0.9%. AFTER: 0 in 9 (load 1.24-9.00). 0-in-9 vs 0-in-9 is not evidence and none is claimed - stated in the banner, packet section 3.4 and the harness comment. MECHANISM, which CORRECTS the open item rather than confirming it: Chromium's scheduled localStorage commit for a busy session here is 43.8/48.3/54.0s out, reproducible to 25ms (a budget, not a race), and the app is gone ~50ms after window.close() (12 launches, 49-51ms; O50's 99ms was its 100ms poll granularity, so we agree). BUT window.close() COMMITS THE AREA so that timer never applies: with the close, the last write is on disk 20/20 sessions; with the close line deleted, 3 of 4 lose it - exactly the three whose own commit is 44-54s away. FIX: verify the artifact after the process is gone - a unique marker read out of the profile's leveldb, one read, no wait, no retry (a dead process writes nothing, and a bounded retry is the same mistake with a longer timeout). Run time unchanged 171-173s. REJECTED with reasons: session.flushStorageData (main-process only, and it REQUESTS rather than confirms - the vacuous-guard shape); a pre-close wait that WORKED and was removed because it cost 173s -> 320s waiting out a timer the close pre-empts, with two commits left on the branch on purpose. SECOND DEFECT, worse: cdp() settled only on a matching message, never on close/error, so a dying target left a promise unsettled, node's loop emptied, and the run exited 0 at ~45% WITH NO SUMMARY - a sweep reading exit codes records a PASS. Closed twice: cdp() rejects in-flight by name, and installSummaryNet forces exit 3 on any exit without a summary. A FALSE ZERO nearly became the finding: the first pass watched ~/.config/aurora (the owner's packaged profile) while the harness writes ~/.config/Electron, giving a clean reproducible wrong '0 of 6'; the resolver now reads the profile from /proc/<pid>/fd and REFUSES between two candidates. Guard proven: plant on the committed artifact, first run, session B false -> rc=2 at the teardown that lost the data; on the diagnostic-only arm the run still printed 52/52 with three sessions' writes lost, so the new check is strictly stronger than waitRestored. New gate test/support/storage-flush.test.ts, 25 rows in npm test, red-first on three mutations. The agent hit the edited-mid-measurement error once, caught it, DISCARDED the batch and re-ran the before arm from scratch. npm test after the merge: 7 failed / 6690 passed / 7 skipped - the same 7 that fail on master, all aeon/empyrean tip-reading rows the vendor parcel is closing; no new failure. headline: The plane-swap effect can be authored now - and building the panel found three MORE places where the code assumed there were only two kinds of effect, including one that would have created the wrong kind on first use.
matters: Two fields, an address shown as what it means rather than a bare number, and a sentence saying this one runs in every build unlike its neighbour. The dropdown no longer admits it cannot be authored, because now it can. The part worth your attention is that this is the THIRD round of the same fault. Two hours ago a third kind of effect appeared and broke three things in the panel I had just shipped. Those were fixed. Building this panel found three more the earlier sweep missed - and the worst of them meant that the very first time anyone switched a preset to the new kind, they would silently have got the OLD kind instead, because the code said 'if not this, then the only other one'. That is now impossible by construction rather than by care: the kinds live in one list, and adding a fourth would fail loudly at startup rather than quietly doing the wrong thing. It also proves undo in BOTH directions, which the previous panel did not - the way OUT is what you reach for when you change your mind.

The dropdown's '(not authorable here yet)' is gone BY CONSTRUCTION - that string is printed by rasterChannelSeedRefusal and the channel now has a seed. target shown as hex beside decimal in three places, with $E000/VRAM_PLANE_B PARSED out of the schema's worked example (BASE_SWAP_NAMED_TARGETS, guarded decimal-equals-hex, in range, on granule); no other address is ever named. headline: The editor no longer points you at a scroll rate the game cannot hold - and the test written to catch that mistake caught a version of the same mistake inside itself.
matters: A negative scroll rate has never been able to reach a ROM - the engine writes the value into a field that cannot hold a negative number, and nobody noticed because every rate ever authored was positive until ours. Our panel made that worse rather than better: when you typed a rate it could not represent, it helpfully named the nearest ones you COULD have - and one of those was negative, so it pointed you straight at a wall, with the authority of a fix. Now it still names them, because they are genuinely the nearest, and it adds that a negative one does not reach the game yet. Only if you are actually using a negative value; a positive one shows nothing at all. And the warning removes ITSELF when the engine is fixed - not when someone says it is fixed, but when our test reads their code and sees the fix. The nice part: while proving the warning would come back if the problem returned, the test found that it was silently reading the real value through a stub - so it would have passed while proving nothing. That is the exact failure this whole day has been about, found inside the thing built to prevent it.

headline: Correcting myself: I wrote that the downward scroll rate 'reaches the hardware'. What was actually proven is that the ROM CONTAINS the right number - nobody has watched the machine consume it.
matters: A small phrase in my summary two hours ago, and worth fixing because it is the exact distinction this whole evening has been about. What the engine lane's test does is compare WHICH LINES CHANGED between two builds - and for the span check it deliberately compares two flat runs, so it proves where the effect starts and stops and says nothing at all about direction. Separately, the number stored in the ROM was decoded and matches what our editor wrote. Both are real results. Neither is 'the machine scrolled downward'. Proving that needs a different test - sampling the VALUES along the run and checking they descend by the exact step, not merely that something moved - and the engine lane has booked it and is deliberately not running it tonight under load. The code comment beside the constant already said this correctly; only my summary to you was loose.

headline: A sentence the editor shows you about where a scroll effect lands now says whose reading it is - because it turns out nobody has asked the hardware.
matters: When you set up a ramp effect, the panel tells you which screen lines it will actually appear on. That explanation was written as plain fact. It is not one. The number comes from reading one emulator core; the older core reads it one line earlier on the identical ROM, and it cannot be used to settle the argument because it disagrees with ITSELF between two identical boots. The newer core's own notes say this timing is still an interim model. So the honest sentence is 'this is what our instrument reads today', and that is what the tooltip now says - built from the contract's own words, with a check that refuses to load if anyone quietly deletes the attribution or retypes it by hand. The numbers themselves did not move and nothing you have authored changes. The sweep also found thirteen other places across twelve files stating it as settled, two of which I had not thought to look for: one named the WRONG emulator core as the source, and one still repeated a finding the engine lane has since withdrawn - their own follow-up test refuted it, because both effect tiers shifted together, which means the reading instrument changed and the engine never did.

headline: A setting in one panel was quietly changing what a DIFFERENT effect does, and now it tells you - including when it honestly cannot tell.
matters: Turning on V deform for a scene puts the hardware into a per-column scrolling mode. The side effect nobody could see: a ramp effect bound to that same section stops scrolling the full screen width and scrolls a single 16-pixel column instead. You set the two things in two different panels, and nothing connected them. The V-deform row now says so, naming the section and the preset it affects. The half I care about more is what it does when it CANNOT work the answer out - if the preset it would have to check is missing or its file will not parse, it says which of those happened and that the answer is not decidable, rather than guessing the common case. I proved that half by planting the guess ('almost certainly the full width') and watching the check catch it. The sweep also found the preview drawing a full-width split for a document that cannot actually build, and it found that a rule the engine states twice on adjacent lines had only ever been carried across into our editor once. Separately: reels needed nothing - there is no reel surface in the editor at all, which is a real answer rather than a skipped one.

headline: A tooltip in the effects panel was telling you a half-truth about where your effect goes, and it is now the measured version.
matters: When you set a moving anchor, the Movement control's hover text explains what happens if the movement carries the effect outside the band it is allowed to live in. It said the band VANISHES. That is true in one direction only: run off the TOP and the band really does disappear for that frame, but run off the BOTTOM and it is pinned to the edge and stays on screen - deliberately, because something else already covers what is above it. So the text was warning you about a disappearance that, half the time, does not happen. That hover text is not written by us: it is the shared contract's own sentence, shown to you word for word on purpose, so that the editor never invents a rule of its own. The engine was measured, the contract sentence was corrected there, and we took the new bytes. The replacement names no line numbers of its own, so it cannot drift out of date the way the old one silently did.

headline: The Hydrocity-style waterline effect can now be set up in the editor, and it tells you up front which settings the build will reject.
matters: The engine half of the perspective waterline landed on the engine side; this is the half you touch. A layer can now be given the row-remap effect, with the two numbers it needs. Three things about it are easy to get wrong and all three now answer in the editor instead of in a build log: the engine refuses this effect on a scene whose background has nothing to vary (the effect would be not subtle but completely absent), on a scene with no anchor, and on a second layer once one already has it. You meet those while authoring now. One more, which is the honest part: only one of the five sizes actually builds today, because the engine has only one table for it so far. Rather than offer five options and let four of them fail your build, the panel says which one works and why - and that caution is read out of the contract itself, so it disappears on its own the day the engine side adds the rest. Nothing here has produced a real ROM yet: the path from this document to a built game does not exist on the engine side, and I have said so rather than implying it works.

headline: Our own test suite has been going red because someone edited a file in the ENGINE repo, and it is now green end to end.
matters: Two tests were failing, and neither was a bug in this editor. They opened a document out of the engine repo's folder and compared it against a copy of that same document typed into the test. You moved that effect to the top of the frame on the engine side, which was a perfectly ordinary edit, and our suite went red with an error that named no repository at all - so it read like our bug. That is corrosive in a way worth naming: a suite that is permanently a bit red teaches everyone to skim past red. Now the two questions are asked separately. Whether our editor can read the document is checked against a copy pinned here at a named engine revision, which cannot be disturbed by anyone editing anything. Whether that copy is still what the engine ships is a different check that goes and looks, says which revision it is comparing, and when it cannot reach the engine repo at all it says so out loud instead of quietly passing. I proved that half by deleting the engine repo from its view entirely and watching the right things pass and the right things announce they could not measure. One thing found on the way that is NOT ours to settle: the shared contract repo and the engine repo currently disagree about what this effect's value should be. We are correct either way and deliberately take no side.

headline: Two buttons could throw your work away on one misclick with no undo and no warning. Both now ask - and only when there is something to lose.
matters: The sprite size chips and New sit in the option bar next to tools you use constantly, and pressing one replaced the whole sprite, threw away its undo history, AND told the app there was nothing unsaved - so the dot went out and nothing downstream would ever have asked you about it either. Clear in the Chunks section emptied the whole library the same way; Ctrl+Z did not bring it back. Both now ask first. The important half is the word ONLY: if the document is clean there is no dialog at all, which is exactly what you chose the last time you ruled on one of these buttons - you took no dialog THEN because that wipe was one undo away, and these are not. It would have been easy to ship a version that always asks; that passes every obvious test and quietly overturns your preference, so the test I care about here is the one that presses the button on a clean document and proves no dialog was ever on screen. It uses the same dialog the app already shows when you close a tab with unsaved work, so there is nothing new to learn. Worth knowing: this was decided in your place under the standing delegation, not by you, and it is yours to overturn on sight.

headline: The dialog we added tonight is safe only by accident, and the ordinary fix for a different problem would turn it into a silent sprite-wipe.
matters: The confirm dialog now guards six places, and when it opens it puts keyboard focus on nothing at all. That is an accessibility gap - if you drive by keyboard you have to tab into it to answer it - and it is also the ONLY reason the app is currently safe. I had it proved rather than argued: adding autofocus to the dialog's destructive button, which is four characters and exactly what anyone fixing the accessibility gap would type, makes a single press of the space bar wipe your sprite in the real running app - five frames down to one, everything you painted gone, undo history cleared, and the unsaved marker reset so nothing afterwards would ever have asked you about it. Nothing is on fire: the app as it stands is safe, and the six new checks confirm focus lands nowhere dangerous after the dialog closes any of the three ways. But the safety is an accident nobody chose, and another piece of work already in the codebase names this exact dialog as its next target. It is a decision for you, written up with a recommendation: focus the SAFE button, which is both more accessible and strictly safer than today.

headline: Every test rig in the repo was measured for the false-red defect, and the tidy rule we had for which ones were affected turns out to be wrong.
matters: A while back a rig was found reporting FAILURE while every one of its checks passed - it was deleting a file belonging to the wrapper that launched it. That was fixed, but only ten of the rigs had ever been measured, and the rest were left as an honest gap. All 133 have now been run. Thirty-six of them hit the condition. The useful part is that the neat rule we had for predicting which ones - 'the ones that tear down a certain way, by construction' - is false: two of them tear down that way and are fine, because their processes had already exited. Worse for confidence, one rig in the supposedly-safe group DID hit it, on one run out of four - the slow run. Its teardown waits a fixed one and a half seconds and never checks whether anything actually stopped. So a single clean run of one of these proves nothing, which cuts against this measurement's own clean results as much as against the old ones, and the agent said so about its own numbers rather than only about the earlier ones. Three rigs could not be measured at all because they run past fifteen minutes; those are recorded as unmeasured, not as passes.
detail: Merge df81fca3, branch parcel/o78-residual-census tip ec7782df, 10 commits, ~3h wall. headline: A test rig was deleting a project directory 1.5 seconds after asking the app to quit, without ever checking that it had.

headline: The 'change a slider and watch the game change' feature now has a written ask to the engine lane - and it needs far less from them than we thought.
matters: It was only ever a phrase on my own board, so it would have vanished at the next session boundary. Reading the engine's code turned up that most of it is already built: the game can already swap a whole effect setup mid-play from a debug path. What is missing is somewhere for the editor to write one, and a way to say 'now'. I also wrote down what it will NOT buy - live art still needs a build - so the engine lane can decline on an honest price rather than discovering the limit later.
detail: A12-ENGINE-ASK. Packet docs/reviews/2026-09-04-a12-engine-ask.md, aurora 51d3590 (pushed; git ls-remote confirms master moved, not the push's own output). Every aeon citation read at origin/master 75da5e1c via `git show <rev>:<path>`, never the sibling path. The seam: Effects_InstallPreset (engine/effects/preset.emp:279, TOTAL BINDING, runs from the main loop at the crossing site parallax.emp:1115) takes a0 = Sec* and resolves sec_effects; Debug_PresetCycleHotkey (games/sonic4/test/ojz_scroll_test.emp:2630, START+A, DEBUG only) already resolves an arbitrary Sec*, stands down on a null sec_effects, calls it and repaints a readout. So the ask is two things only: a 46-byte RAM EffectsPreset shadow and a bus-writable one-shot arm word. Size checked on both sides rather than assumed: RASTER_MAX_PATCH = 4 (raster_dsl.emp:2131, with an ensure at scene_dsl.emp:56), schema maxItems 4, and Aurora's EFFECTS_PRESET_MAX_PATCH is DERIVED from the schema (effects-preset.ts:2373, :2544) so it cannot drift - had it been 8 the shadow would be 54 B and the packet's arithmetic wrong. Scope boundary stated in the packet: six preset fields are pointers, so the shadow buys the inline words (patch_world_ys, patch_motion, transition - exactly BandPresetPanel's World Y/Movement/Travel/Cycle/Start at) plus swapping among already-built ROM blobs, and NOT new blob content. Whether those pointers could aim at Aurora-written RAM is aeon's question (DMA/alignment/bank assumptions) and is deliberately not asserted. Board correction in the same pass: EW-BOUNDARY-AUTHORING deleted as stale - it read 'nobody can author a moving band in Aurora at all', and the anchor-mover authoring surface landed 2026-09-03 (lane-log 09:38:33Z); verified by reading BandPresetPanel.tsx:750-800 (World Y, Movement, Travel, Cycle, Start at, AnchorSweepPreview) rather than by trusting the log. Fourth instance of a row outliving its fix on this board.

headline: The editor now tells you when a band's up-and-down movement is too big to fit the strip of screen it lives in - and refuses to tell you the opposite.
matters: Until now nothing in Aurora knew how much room a band actually has, so you could set a movement six times too large and find out only by building and looking. It now says so as you type. The deliberate half: when the movement DOES fit, it stays quiet rather than showing a tick - because where the movement sits on screen depends on where the player is standing, so 'it fits' is something nobody can honestly promise at author time. A green tick we could not honour would be worse than saying nothing.
